## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T$ be an invertible bimeasurable probability-preserving transformation on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ such that $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$ implies $Q(A)\in\{0,1\}$. Let $X_0\in L^2(Q)$ be real and centered, put $X_k=X_0\circ T^k$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$, and put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$. Suppose
$$\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]\|_2<\infty.$$
Then the $L^2$ series $H_0=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]$ converges. Put $H_k=H_0\circ T^k$ and $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$. The $D_k$ are stationary square-integrable martingale differences for $\mathcal F_k$, and for $n\ge1$,
$$S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k+H_0-H_n,\qquad \|H_0-H_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2.$$
With $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$,
$$S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2),$$
including $\tau^2=0$. If additionally $\sum_{j\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)|<\infty$, then
$$\tau^2=\mathbb E[X_0^2]+2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the invertible probability-preserving ergodic transformation $T$, centered real $X_0\in L^2(Q)$, its stationary translates, natural past filtration, and the displayed summability assumption.

[A1] AC supplies the inherited choices for the following conditional-expectation and limit suppliers. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] Conditional expectation is linear, preserves expectation and constants, and contracts the real $L^2$ norm. ([[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]], [[cor-conditional-lp-contraction]])

[F2] Conditional expectations satisfy the tower property and allow a known measurable factor to be taken out when the input and the required products are integrable. ([[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]], [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]])

[F3] Under countable choice $L^2$ is complete. ([[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]])

[F4] Square-integrable products satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]])

[F5] A stationary integrable process with ergodic canonical shift has averages converging almost surely to its expectation. Ergodicity requires invariant events to have probability zero or one. ([[thm-stationary-process-birkhoff-ergodic-limit]], [[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]])

[F6] A square-integrable martingale-difference array with terminal conditional variance clock tending to $1$ in probability and vanishing unconditional Lindeberg sums has terminal sum converging to $N(0,1)$. ([[thm-martingale-central-limit-theorem]])

[F7] Dominated convergence passes limits through integrals dominated by an integrable function. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F8] $L^2$ convergence implies convergence in probability; a perturbation tending to zero in probability preserves a weak limit; continuous scaling preserves weak convergence. ([[thm-lp-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]], [[thm-converging-together-lemma]], [[thm-continuous-mapping-theorem]])

[F9] Variance and covariance are centered second and product moments. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

## Proof

1.1 For an integrable $Z$ and any integer $k$, the variable $\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$ measurable because the pullback of $\mathcal F_0$ by $T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$. Every event in $\mathcal F_k$ is the pullback of an event in $\mathcal F_0$, since $T$ is invertible and bimeasurable. Changing variables under the probability-preserving bijection $T^k$ proves that the integrals of this candidate and $Z\circ T^k$ agree over every $\mathcal F_k$ event. Uniqueness of conditional expectation therefore gives $\mathbb E[Z\circ T^k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ as almost-everywhere classes. [A1, F1, given]

1.2 By summability and [F3], the partial sums defining $H_0$ are Cauchy in $L^2(\mathcal F_0)$ and have a limit there. Composition with $T^k$ is an $L^2$ isometry, so step 1.1 yields $H_k=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_k]$ in $L^2$, with $H_k$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $\|H_k\|_2=\|H_0\|_2$. Representatives may be fixed for the countably many indices; discard a countable union of null sets for their identities. [A1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct]

1.3 By [F1], conditional expectation is continuous in $L^2$. Apply [F2]'s tower property to the partial sums in step 1.2 and pass to the $L^2$ limit to obtain $\mathbb E[H_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=H_{k-1}-\mathbb E[X_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$. Thus $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$ is square-integrable and $\mathcal F_k$ measurable, with $\mathbb E[D_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=0$. Also $D_k=D_1\circ T^{k-1}$, so the differences are stationary. Summing their defining identity gives $S_n=M_n+R_n$, where $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$, $R_n=H_0-H_n$, and $\|R_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2$. In particular $R_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability by [F8]. [F1, F2, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Put $q_0=\mathbb E[D_1^2\mid\mathcal F_0]$. It is nonnegative, integrable, and has expectation $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$ by [F1]. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=q_0\circ T^{k-1}$. The map $\omega\mapsto(q_0(T^j\omega))_{j\ge0}$ intertwines $T$ with the canonical one-sided shift. Hence a shift-invariant event for this process pulls back to a $T$-invariant event modulo null sets, whose probability is zero or one by the assumed ergodicity. The process is stationary, integrable and ergodic, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\to\tau^2$ almost surely. The limiting variance is therefore a constant. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, given]

2.2 If $\tau^2>0$, let $Z_{n,k}=D_k/(\tau\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$, and let $Z_{n,k}=0$ for $k>n$; use the filtration $\mathcal F_{n,k}=\mathcal F_{\min(k,n)}$ for $k\ge0$. Step 1.3 makes each row a square-integrable martingale-difference row. The row sums and clocks are eventually constant, and step 2.1 shows their terminal clocks converge almost surely to $1$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity gives $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\tau\sqrt n\}}]\to0$ by [F7]. Thus [F6] gives $M_n/(\tau\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Scaling and the perturbation in step 1.3 give $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ by [F8]. [A1, F6, F7, F8, step 1.3, step 2.1, construct]

2.3 If $\tau^2=0$, stationarity implies $\mathbb E[D_k^2]=0$ for every $k$, so $M_n=0$ almost surely. Step 1.3 gives $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability. The constant sequence $0$ has weak limit the point mass $N(0,0)$; [F8] transfers that limit to $S_n/\sqrt n$. This establishes the asserted CLT in both variance cases. [F8, step 1.3, step 2.2, given]

3.1 Suppose the additional covariance summability holds, and put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-j/n)\gamma_j\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j$, by [F7] on counting measure with summable dominator $|\gamma_j|$. For $i<j$, $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$ measurable, so [F2], [F4], and step 1.3 give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E[M_n^2]=n\tau^2$. The identity $S_n=M_n+R_n$ and [F4] imply $|\mathbb E[S_n^2]-n\tau^2|/n\le\|R_n\|_2^2/n+2\|R_n\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$, since $\|R_n\|_2$ is bounded. All $S_n$ are centered, so [F9] identifies the two variance limits and proves the stated covariance formula, including $\tau^2=0$. [F2, F4, F7, F9, step 1.3, given] ∎

## Source notes

The absolutely summable projection assumption permits an exact $L^2$ coboundary series, so no maximal martingale approximation theorem is imported. The deterministic variance follows from the explicitly assumed ergodicity and its factor argument. The covariance identity is obtained from second moments, independently of convergence in distribution.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_{n,k},\mathcal F_{n,k})$ be a square-integrable martingale-difference array such that, for every $n$, $M_{n,m}$ and $\Gamma_{n,m}$ converge almost surely as $m\to\infty$ to finite limits $M_{n,\infty}$ and $\Gamma_{n,\infty}$. If
$$\Gamma_{n,\infty}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{in probability}$$
and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$L_n(\varepsilon):=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2 1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]\longrightarrow0,$$
then $M_{n,\infty}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Let $1\le p<\infty$. If $X_n\to X$ in $L^p$, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: For an integrable $Z$ and any integer $k$, the variable $\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$ measurable because the pullback of $\mathcal F_0$ by $T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$. Every event in $\mathcal F_k$ is the pullback of an event in $\mathcal F_0$, since $T$ is invertible and bimeasurable. Changing variables under the probability-preserving bijection $T^k$ proves that the integrals of this candidate and $Z\circ T^k$ agree over every $\mathcal F_k$ event. Uniqueness of conditional expectation therefore gives $\mathbb E[Z\circ T^k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ as almost-everywhere classes.

By summability and [F3], the partial sums defining $H_0$ are Cauchy in $L^2(\mathcal F_0)$ and have a limit there. Composition with $T^k$ is an $L^2$ isometry, so step 1.1 yields $H_k=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_k]$ in $L^2$, with $H_k$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $\|H_k\|_2=\|H_0\|_2$. Representatives may be fixed for the countably many indices; discard a countable union of null sets for their identities.

By [F1], conditional expectation is continuous in $L^2$. Apply [F2]'s tower property to the partial sums in step 1.2 and pass to the $L^2$ limit to obtain $\mathbb E[H_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=H_{k-1}-\mathbb E[X_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$. Thus $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$ is square-integrable and $\mathcal F_k$ measurable, with $\mathbb E[D_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=0$. Also $D_k=D_1\circ T^{k-1}$, so the differences are stationary. Summing their defining identity gives $S_n=M_n+R_n$, where $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$, $R_n=H_0-H_n$, and $\|R_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2$. In particular $R_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability by [F8].

Put $q_0=\mathbb E[D_1^2\mid\mathcal F_0]$. It is nonnegative, integrable, and has expectation $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$ by [F1]. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=q_0\circ T^{k-1}$. The map $\omega\mapsto(q_0(T^j\omega))_{j\ge0}$ intertwines $T$ with the canonical one-sided shift. Hence a shift-invariant event for this process pulls back to a $T$-invariant event modulo null sets, whose probability is zero or one by the assumed ergodicity. The process is stationary, integrable and ergodic, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\to\tau^2$ almost surely. The limiting variance is therefore a constant.

If $\tau^2>0$, let $Z_{n,k}=D_k/(\tau\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$, and let $Z_{n,k}=0$ for $k>n$; use the filtration $\mathcal F_{n,k}=\mathcal F_{\min(k,n)}$ for $k\ge0$. Step 1.3 makes each row a square-integrable martingale-difference row. The row sums and clocks are eventually constant, and step 2.1 shows their terminal clocks converge almost surely to $1$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity gives $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\tau\sqrt n\}}]\to0$ by [F7]. Thus [F6] gives $M_n/(\tau\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Scaling and the perturbation in step 1.3 give $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ by [F8].

If $\tau^2=0$, stationarity implies $\mathbb E[D_k^2]=0$ for every $k$, so $M_n=0$ almost surely. Step 1.3 gives $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability. The constant sequence $0$ has weak limit the point mass $N(0,0)$; [F8] transfers that limit to $S_n/\sqrt n$. This establishes the asserted CLT in both variance cases.

Suppose the additional covariance summability holds, and put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-j/n)\gamma_j\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j$, by [F7] on counting measure with summable dominator $|\gamma_j|$. For $i<j$, $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$ measurable, so [F2], [F4], and step 1.3 give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E[M_n^2]=n\tau^2$. The identity $S_n=M_n+R_n$ and [F4] imply $|\mathbb E[S_n^2]-n\tau^2|/n\le\|R_n\|_2^2/n+2\|R_n\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$, since $\|R_n\|_2$ is bounded. All $S_n$ are centered, so [F9] identifies the two variance limits and proves the stated covariance formula, including $\tau^2=0$.

## Example

Set $\delta=1$ and $b_n=\lfloor n^{1/2}\rfloor$ for $n\ge2$. This sequence
fails one Flegal–Jones batch-size condition,
$n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3/b_n\to0$. The example establishes
inapplicability of this sufficient condition only; it does not imply that the
OBM estimator is inconsistent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^{1/2}\rfloor$ and the lower-growth batch-size premise retained in the corrected Flegal–Jones OBM contract.

[F1] The Flegal–Jones batch-size contract for exponent $\delta$ includes the lower-growth limit $n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3/b_n\to0$. ([[def-flegal-jones-obm-batch-size-conditions]])

[F2] The OBM estimator uses overlapping batch means of integer length $b_n<n$. ([[alg-overlapping-batch-means-mcse]])

## Verification
1.1 For $n\ge2$, $n^{1/2}-1<b_n\le n^{1/2}$, so $b_n/n^{1/2}\to1$. Thus $n^{2/3}(\log n)^3/b_n\sim n^{1/6}(\log n)^3\to\infty$, which violates the required limit in [F1] at $\delta=1$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $1\le b_n\le n^{1/2}<n$ for $n\ge2$, the finite OBM procedure in [F2] is defined. Step 1.1 establishes failure of one source sufficient condition only, not inconsistency of the estimator. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge2$, $n^{1/2}-1<b_n\le n^{1/2}$, so $b_n/n^{1/2}\to1$. Thus $n^{2/3}(\log n)^3/b_n\sim n^{1/6}(\log n)^3\to\infty$, which violates the required limit in [F1] at $\delta=1$.
Since $1\le b_n\le n^{1/2}<n$ for $n\ge2$, the finite OBM procedure in [F2] is defined. Step 1.1 establishes failure of one source sufficient condition only, not inconsistency of the estimator.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and all hypotheses in the Statement. Denote an everywhere finite measurable envelope in the geometric-ergodicity hypothesis by $M_0$, with rate $r_0\in(0,1)$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed for the small-set supplier and the canonical path-space and Markov suppliers below.

[F1] [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]: $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M_0(x)r_0^n$ for every $x$ and $n\ge1$, with $M_0$ finite and measurable.

[F2] [[lem-countably-generated-kernel-stable-sub-sigma-field]]: a real measurable observable belongs to a countably generated sub-sigma-field on which the kernel restricts, with the same iterated transitions on restricted events and the restricted invariant law.

[F3] [[lem-phi-irreducible-chain-has-small-set]]: a countably generated irreducible chain has a positive-irreducibility-measure small set $D$, with a minorizing probability $\nu_0$ satisfying $\nu_0(D)>0$.

[F4] [[lem-geometric-split-renewal-gives-integrable-hitting-time]]: a one-step small set of positive invariant mass, whose minorizing-law return probabilities converge geometrically, has a stationary-integrable exponential entrance-time moment.

[F5] [[cor-canonical-markov-chain-on-path-space]]: under AC, the original kernel has canonical chains from every initial law.

[F6] [[thm-discrete-strong-markov-property]]: bounded future-path functionals obey the Markov identity at stopping times.

[F7] [[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]: irreducibility relative to a nonzero measure means that each positive-measure measurable set is accessible from every state at some positive time.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and the envelope $M_0,r_0$ in [F1], with AC [A1].

1.1 Apply [F2] to $M_0$ to obtain a countably generated $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal X$, the restricted kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$, and invariant probability $\pi_{\mathcal G}=\pi|_{\mathcal G}$. If $B\in\mathcal G$ has $\pi_{\mathcal G}(B)>0$, [F1] implies $P^n(x,B)>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for each $x$, because $M_0(x)$ is finite. Thus $P_{\mathcal G}$ is $\pi_{\mathcal G}$-irreducible by [F7]. Applying [F3] on this countably generated space gives an $m\ge1$, a $D\in\mathcal G$ with $\pi(D)>0$, a probability $\nu_0$ on $\mathcal G$ with $\nu_0(D)>0$, and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $P_{\mathcal G}^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon_0\nu_0$ on $D$. No small-set assertion on the original sigma-field is being made. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7, given]

1.2 Since $M_0$ is finite everywhere, $D\cap\{M_0\le K\}$ increases to $D$ as the positive integer $K$ increases. Choose $K$ so $C=D\cap\{M_0\le K\}$ has both $\pi(C)>0$ and $\nu_0(C)>0$. Choose a finite integer $L\ge K$ and put $a=\nu_0(M_0\le L)>0$, $\nu(B)=\nu_0(B\cap\{M_0\le L\})/a$. Choose $0<\epsilon<\min(1,\epsilon_0a)$. For $Q=P_{\mathcal G}^m$ this gives $Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu$ on $C$, $\nu(M_0)\le L$, and $M_0\le K$ on $C$. [F1, step 1.1, choose, construct]

2.1 For $n\ge1$, the restricted-iteration identity in [F2] and [F1] give
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le\int M_0(x)r_0^{mn}\nu(dx)\le L(r_0^m)^n.$$
For $n=0$ the absolute difference is at most $1$. Therefore [F4] applies with constant $\max(1,L)$ and rate $r_0^m$. It supplies $s>1$ and a measurable $H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^\sigma]$, where $\sigma=\inf\{j\ge0:X_{jm}\in C\}$, such that $\pi(H)<\infty$. Indeed the skeleton path restricted to $\mathcal G$ under the full canonical $P$-chain has the $Q$-chain law: its finite-dimensional cylinder probabilities agree by the iterated-kernel identity in [F2]. Thus the same $H$ is the entrance-time moment for the original chain of [F5]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.2]

2.2 Choose $\max(r_0,s^{-1/m})<r_1<1$, and set $S=m\sigma$ and $K_1=\max(1,K)$. Fix $A\in\mathcal X$ and $n\ge1$. On $\{S\le n\}$, decompose into the finitely many events $\{S=j\}$ and use [F6] to replace the conditional terminal indicator by $P^{n-j}(X_j,A)$. Since $X_j\in C$, [F1] bounds its difference from $\pi(A)$ by $K_1r_0^{n-j}$; when $j=n$, use $|1_A(X_n)-\pi(A)|\le1\le K_1$. On $\{S>n\}$ use the bound $1$. Subtracting $\pi(A)$ on these two events gives
$$|P^n(x,A)-\pi(A)|\le\mathbb P_x(S>n)+K_1\mathbb E_x[r_0^{n-S};S\le n]\le(1+K_1)r_1^nH(x).$$
For the final inequality, $r_1^{-S}\le s^\sigma$, and on $S\le n$ one has $r_0^{n-S}\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$; on $S>n$, $1\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$. This argument is for each original measurable event $A$, so taking its supremum controls the full original total variation and does not require measurability of a total-variation supremum. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 The measurable set $N=\{H=\infty\}$ is $\pi$-null by step 2.1. Define $M_1(x)=(1+K_1)H(x)$ for $x\notin N$ and $M_1(x)=M_0(x)$ for $x\in N$. It is measurable and finite everywhere, and $\pi(M_1)<\infty$. Off $N$, step 2.2 gives the desired bound with rate $r_1$; on $N$, [F1] gives it because $r_0<r_1$. Taking $M=M_1$ and $r=r_1$ proves the full Statement. AC was used precisely through [F3] and the path-space and Markov suppliers [F4]–[F6]. [A1, F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. There is a countably generated sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ such that $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $P$, restricted to events in $\mathcal G$, is a probability kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$ on $(X,\mathcal G)$. For every $n\ge0$, $x\in X$, and $B\in\mathcal G$,
$$P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B).$$
If $\pi$ is invariant for $P$, then $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ is invariant for $P_{\mathcal G}$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel, and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. ## Statement

Assume AC. Let $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ be real random variables and $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kY_i$, with $S_0=0$. Suppose on a probability-space extension with the original process as marginal there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, constants $\sigma\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1/2$, and finite random constants $K,N$ such that almost surely
$$|S_k-\sigma B(k)|\le K k^\alpha\log k\qquad(k\ge N).$$
Let $(b_n)$ be deterministic positive integers with $b_n<n$ eventually and
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\to0,\qquad \sum_{n=2}^\infty(b_n/n)^c<\infty\quad\text{for some real }c\ge1,$$
$$\frac{b_n\log n}{n}\to0,\qquad\frac{n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2}{b_n}\to0.$$
For the exact estimator of [[alg-overlapping-batch-means-mcse]], applied to $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$,
$$\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{OBM},n}^2=\frac{nb_n}{(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n-b_n}\left(\frac{S_{j+b_n}-S_j}{b_n}-\frac{S_n}{n}\right)^2\longrightarrow\sigma^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
No stationarity, independence of $B$ from $(Y_i)$, or monotonicity of $b_n$ or $n/b_n$ is required. The conclusion includes $\sigma=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the original process and its Brownian approximation on the stated extension, the constants $\sigma,\alpha$, and the deterministic batch sequence with all displayed numerical hypotheses.

[A1] AC is assumed as in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and the Brownian and Gaussian interfaces.

[F1] Brownian motion starts at zero and has independent normal increments with variance equal to interval length. [[def-brownian-motion]]

[F2] A centered Gaussian quadratic form satisfies the dimension-free even-moment bound for every positive integer $r$. [[lem-gaussian-quadratic-form-centered-even-moment-bound]]

[F3] For a nonnegative random variable $X$ and $a>0$, $\Pr(X\ge a)\le EX/a$. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]

[F4] Events with summable probabilities occur only finitely often almost surely. [[thm-first-borel-cantelli]]

[F5] The standard-normal Mills upper bound $\Pr(Z>x)\le e^{-x^2/2}/(x\sqrt{2\pi})$, together with symmetry and the normal density, gives $\Pr(|Z|\ge x)\le2e^{-x^2/2}$ for $x\ge1$. [[lem-two-sided-mills-bounds-for-standard-normal-tail]]

[F6] The Euclidean norm is a norm and satisfies $|\|x\|_2-\|y\|_2|\le\|x-y\|_2$. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[lem-reverse-triangle-inequality-in-a-normed-space]]

[F7] The finite OBM algorithm uses the displayed denominator and overlapping batch means. [[alg-overlapping-batch-means-mcse]]

## Proof

1.1 Work first on the extension. For each sufficiently large $n$ write $b=b_n$, $m=n-b+1$, $U_i=B(i)-B(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le n$, and $D_j=B(j+b)-B(j)$ for $0\le j\le n-b$. By [F1], the $U_i$ are independent standard normals. If $h_j$ indicates coordinates $j+1,\ldots,j+b$, then $Q_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jD_j^2=U^TA_nU$ where $A_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jh_jh_j^T$. At most $b$ windows contain a fixed pair of coordinates, and none does if their separation is at least $b$. Hence $0\le(A_n)_{ik}\le1/n$, $(A_n)_{ik}=0$ when $|i-k|\ge b$, $\operatorname{tr}A_n=m/n$, and $\sum_{i,k}(A_n)_{ik}^2\le(2b-1)/n\le2b/n$. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose an integer $r\ge c$. By [F2] and [F3], for every $\eta>0$, $\Pr(|Q_n-m/n|>\eta)\le C_r\eta^{-2r}(2b_n/n)^r$. These probabilities are summable since $b_n/n<1$ eventually, $r\ge c$ and $\sum_n(b_n/n)^c<\infty$. Applying [F4] for each $\eta=1,1/2,1/3,\ldots$ and intersecting the resulting countable family of full-probability events gives $Q_n-m/n\to0$ almost surely. Since $m/n\to1$, $Q_n\to1$ almost surely. No independence between different $n$ is used. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and [F5], $\Pr(|B(n)|>\sqrt{6n\log n})\le2n^{-3}$ for $n\ge2$. Thus [F4] gives $B(n)^2/n\le6\log n$ eventually almost surely. Put $V_j=D_j-(b/n)B(n)$ and $W_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jV_j^2$. Applying [F6] to the vectors $(V_j)/\sqrt{nb}$ and $(D_j)/\sqrt{nb}$ gives $|\sqrt{W_n}-\sqrt{Q_n}|\le[(m/n)(b/n)(B(n)^2/n)]^{1/2}\to0$, using $(b_n/n)\log n\to0$. Consequently $W_n\to1$ almost surely. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Set $R_k=S_k-\sigma B(k)$ and $R_0=0$. On the full event of the given approximation, enlarge its finite random constant to absorb all finitely many early errors. Since $k^\alpha\log k$ is increasing for integers $k\ge2$, this gives a finite random $K'$ with $\max_{0\le k\le n}|R_k|\le K'n^\alpha\log n$ for every sufficiently large $n$. For every window, $S_{j+b}-S_j-(b/n)S_n=\sigma V_j+E_{n,j}$ where $E_{n,j}=R_{j+b}-R_j-(b/n)R_n$. Therefore $|E_{n,j}|\le3K'n^\alpha\log n$ simultaneously for all windows, and $H_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jE_{n,j}^2\le9(K')^2(m/n)n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2/b_n\to0$. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.2 Put $T_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_j(S_{j+b}-S_j-(b/n)S_n)^2$. By [F6] and $\sigma\ge0$, $|\sqrt{T_n}-\sigma\sqrt{W_n}|\le\sqrt{H_n}\to0$. Hence $T_n\to\sigma^2$ almost surely. This argument divides neither by $\sigma$ nor by $T_n$, so it also proves the zero-variance case. [F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

4.1 By [F7], $\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{OBM},n}^2=n^2T_n/[(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)]$. This deterministic multiplier tends to one because $b_n/n\to0$, and step 3.2 proves the desired limit on the extension. The event that this sequence of finite measurable functions of $(Y_i)$ converges to $\sigma^2$ depends only on the original process. Its probability under the extension equals its probability under the original marginal, so that probability is one for the original process as well. Arbitrarily defining the estimator at any finitely many indices with inadmissible batches does not affect its limit. [F7, step 3.2, given, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume AC. For every positive integer $r$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, depending only on $r$, such that for every integer $n\ge1$, independent standard-normal variables $U_1,\ldots,U_n$, and real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $A$,
$$E\left|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^{2r}\le C_r\left(\sum_{i,k=1}^n A_{ik}^2\right)^r.$$
In particular $E(U^TAU)=\operatorname{tr}A$. The matrix may be singular or indefinite.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $V$ be a normed space. For all $x,y\in V$,
$$\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le \|x-y\|.$$
In particular, the norm map is $1$-Lipschitz for the norm metric.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence, with $|Z_0|\le B$ almost surely for a finite $B$, and suppose
$$\sum_{r=1}^\infty\alpha_Z(r)<\infty.$$
Put $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$. Then its covariance series converges absolutely and
$$\sigma_Z^2=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r=1}^\infty\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(T_n)}n\ge0.$$
Moreover
$$T_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Z^2),$$
including $\sigma_Z^2=0$. Writing $D_Z=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)|$, every finite subset $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right)^2\le D_Z|I|.$$
The strong-mixing coefficient is that of [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the centered strictly stationary bounded sequence, and summability of its strong-mixing coefficients.

[A1] AC is assumed for the characteristic-function convergence criterion and the normal-law supplier. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] Strict stationarity preserves finite-dimensional laws under nonnegative shifts, and the mixing coefficient is the supremum over separated past and future events. ([[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]])

[F2] Bounded real variables from fields with event coefficient $a$ have covariance at most $4ABa$ in absolute value; complex variables obey the analogous bound $16ABa$. ([[lem-strong-mixing-quantile-covariance-bound]])

[F3] Variance and covariance are centered product expectations. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

[F4] Dominated convergence applies on an arbitrary measure space, including counting measure with a summable majorant. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F5] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds absolute product expectations of square-integrable real variables. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]])

[F6] For $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, one has $|r(u)|\le |u|^3/3$ for all real $u$. ([[lem-second-order-characteristic-function-expansion]])

[F7] Under AC the characteristic function of $N(0,s^2)$ is $e^{-s^2t^2/2}$, including $s=0$. ([[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]])

[F8] Under AC, convergence of characteristic functions to that of a specified probability law is equivalent to weak convergence to that law. ([[cor-characteristic-function-criterion-for-weak-convergence]])

## Proof

1.1 Put $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)$. By [F1]–[F2], $|\gamma_r|\le4B^2\alpha_Z(r)$ for $r\ge1$, so $D_Z<\infty$. Expanding the square of a sum indexed by a finite subset $I$ gives its diagonal terms $|I|\gamma_0$ and off-diagonal terms $2\gamma_{j-i}$ for pairs $i<j$ in $I$. For each fixed positive lag there are at most $|I|$ such pairs. Thus the asserted bound $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i)^2\le D_Z|I|$ holds, also for $I=\varnothing$. For a consecutive block, the same expansion gives $\operatorname{Var}(T_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant $2|\gamma_r|$ and [F4] imply convergence to the stated $\sigma_Z^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of variances. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

1.2 Extend the coefficient convention by $\alpha_Z(0)=1$. It is nonincreasing: increasing the separation restricts the future sigma-algebra in [F1]. For ordered indices $i\le j\le k\le l$, write $a=j-i$ and $c=l-k$. If $a>0$, centering of $Z_i$ and [F2] applied to $Z_i$ and $Z_jZ_kZ_l$ give $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(a)$; if $a=0$, the trivial bound $B^4$ suffices. Splitting off the centered last factor gives the same bound with $c$. Therefore $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(\max(a,c))$. There are at most $24$ orderings, at most $p$ choices each for the first index and the middle gap, and $2r+1$ pairs $(a,c)$ with maximum $r$. Hence
$$\mathbb ET_p^4\le96B^4p^2\sum_{r=0}^p(2r+1)\alpha_Z(r)=o(p^3).$$
To justify the last limit, for each fixed $R$, $p^{-1}\sum_{r\le R}r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, whereas $p^{-1}\sum_{R<r\le p}r\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{r>R}\alpha_Z(r)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$; the unweighted part divided by $p$ also tends to zero. Repeated indices are included by the convention at zero. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $\varepsilon_p=\mathbb ET_p^4/p^3$ and $\eta_n=\sup_{p\ge\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor}\varepsilon_p$. By step 1.2, $\eta_n\to0$. For sufficiently large $n$, define $h_n=\min(n^{1/8},\eta_n^{-1/4})$, interpreting the second entry as $+\infty$ if $\eta_n=0$, and ignore the finitely many earlier $n$. Then $h_n\to\infty$, $h_n=o(n^{1/4})$, and $h_n^2\eta_n\to0$. Put $p_n=\lceil\sqrt n h_n\rceil$, $q_n=\lfloor\sqrt n/h_n\rfloor$, and $k_n=\lfloor n/(p_n+q_n)\rfloor$. Thus $p_n,q_n\to\infty$, $p_n/n\to0$, $q_n/p_n\to0$, and $k_np_n/n\to1$. Retain $k_n$ consecutive blocks of length $p_n$, separated by discarded blocks of length $q_n$, and discard the final remainder. Their discarded index set $I_n$ has cardinality at most $k_nq_n+p_n+q_n=o(n)$. Step 1.1 gives $\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in I_n}Z_i\|_2^2\le D_Z|I_n|/n\to0$, controlling all gaps together without asserting their independence. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Summability and monotonicity imply $r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, since $\lfloor r/2\rfloor\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor}^r\alpha_Z(s)$. For large $n$, $n/p_n\le\sqrt n/h_n\le2q_n$, so $k_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\le2q_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\to0$. Let $B_{n,j}$ denote the sum in retained block $j$. At a fixed real frequency $t$, put $U_j=e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}$. Both each factor and every partial product have modulus at most one. The partial product through block $j$ is measurable before the gap preceding block $j+1$, so [F2] bounds the discrepancy in factoring its expectation from $U_{j+1}$ by $16\alpha_Z(q_n)$. Telescoping these factorizations gives
$$\left|\mathbb E e^{it\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}B_{n,j}/\sqrt n}-\prod_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}\right|\le16(k_n-1)\alpha_Z(q_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
This compares characteristic functions only and requires no independent copies or coupling construction. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $W_{n,j}=B_{n,j}/\sqrt n$. These variables are centered and each has the law of $T_{p_n}/\sqrt n$ by stationarity. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 imply $\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2=(k_np_n/n)\operatorname{Var}(T_{p_n})/p_n\to\sigma_Z^2$. Also
$$\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4=\frac{k_n\mathbb ET_{p_n}^4}{n^2}\le\frac{p_n^2}{n}\varepsilon_{p_n}\longrightarrow0,$$

3.2 For fixed $t$, [F6] gives $\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}=1-a_{n,j}+r_{n,j}$, where $a_{n,j}=t^2\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2/2\ge0$ and $\sum_j|r_{n,j}|\le |t|^3\sum_j\mathbb E|W_{n,j}|^3/3\to0$. Step 3.1 gives $\sum_ja_{n,j}\to t^2\sigma_Z^2/2$ and $\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\le(\max_ja_{n,j})\sum_ja_{n,j}\to0$. The elementary real Taylor bound $|1-a-e^{-a}|\le a^2/2$ for $a\ge0$ follows by integrating the second derivative $e^{-a}\le1$ twice. Since both $|\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}|$ and $e^{-a_{n,j}}$ are at most one, the product telescoping inequality now gives
$$\left|\prod_j\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}-e^{-\sum_ja_{n,j}}\right|\le\sum_j|r_{n,j}|+\frac12\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\longrightarrow0.$$

manifest_row.title: Bounded stationary CLT under summable strong mixing
manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence, with $|Z_0|\le B$ almost surely for a finite $B$, and suppose
$$\sum_{r=1}^\infty\alpha_Z(r)<\infty.$$
Put $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$. Then its covariance series converges absolutely and
$$\sigma_Z^2=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r=1}^\infty\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(T_n)}n\ge0.$$
Moreover
$$T_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Z^2),$$
including $\sigma_Z^2=0$. Writing $D_Z=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)|$, every finite subset $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right)^2\le D_Z|I|.$$
The strong-mixing coefficient is that of [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $\mathbb EX=0$ and $\mathbb EX^2=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $\varphi_X(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2)$ as $t\to0$. No third moment or choice axiom is assumed. The same scalar estimates give $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ for every real u. More precisely, for $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, $$|r(u)|\le \min(|u|^3/3,4u^2),\qquad |e^{iu}-1-iu|\le u^2.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\rho_Y(n)<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the centered strictly stationary real sequence $Y$, finite second moment, and $\sum_{n\ge1}\rho_Y(n)<\infty$.

[A1] AC is the inherited assumption of the local extension and martingale CLT suppliers. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] The coefficient $\rho_Y(n)$ bounds absolute correlations between the finite past and separated future. ([[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]])

[F2] The sequence has a two-sided stationary realization $X_k=X_0\circ T^k$ with the same nonnegative-index law and the same maximal-correlation upper bounds for the full past; if $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, its invertible shift is ergodic even for mod-null invariant events. ([[lem-two-sided-stationary-extension-preserves-rho-mixing]])

[F3] Conditional expectation is the $L^2$ orthogonal projection onto the conditioning subspace and preserves ordinary expectation. ([[thm-conditional-expectation-is-the-l2-orthogonal-projection]], [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]])

[F4] For a centered $L^2$ process generated by an invertible probability-preserving ergodic transformation, summability of $\|\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]\|_2$ gives a normal CLT with variance $\mathbb E[D_1^2]\ge0$, including zero; under absolute covariance summability this variance equals the covariance series. ([[thm-summable-l-two-projections-give-stationary-clt]])

[F5] Covariance and variance are centered product and square moments. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

## Proof

1.1 Summability of the nonnegative numbers $\rho_Y(n)$ implies $\rho_Y(n)\to0$. By [F2], realize $Y$ as the nonnegative restriction in law of the two-sided stationary sequence $X_k=X_0\circ T^k$ with an invertible probability-preserving shift $T$ that is ergodic for mod-null invariant events. Its full past $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$ satisfies $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le\rho_Y(n)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}$ for past $U$ and future $V$ separated by $n$. All second moments of the coordinates agree with those of $Y$. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.2 Put $W_j=\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]$ for $j\ge1$. By [F3], $W_j$ is centered and square-integrable and $\mathbb E[W_jX_j]=\mathbb E[W_j^2]$. If $\|W_j\|_2=0$, the bound $\|W_j\|_2\le\rho_Y(j)\|X_0\|_2$ is immediate. Otherwise apply step 1.1's covariance inequality to $W_j$ and $X_j$, divide by $\|W_j\|_2$, and obtain that same bound. Consequently $\sum_{j\ge1}\|\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]\|_2\le\|X_0\|_2\sum_{j\ge1}\rho_Y(j)<\infty$. [F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Step 1.1 applied to the two coordinates gives $|\gamma_j|\le\rho_Y(j)\mathbb E[X_0^2]$ for $j\ge1$; if $X_0$ is constant, both sides vanish. Thus $\sum_{j\ge1}|\gamma_j|<\infty$. All hypotheses of [F4] now hold by steps 1.1 and 1.2. It follows that $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ and $\tau^2=\mathbb E[X_0^2]+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j\ge0$. This includes $\tau^2=0$ and proves absolute covariance convergence. Since $X$ and $Y$ have the same nonnegative-index law, the series is exactly $\sigma_Y^2$ and the finite sums have the original laws. Therefore the asserted nondegenerate and degenerate limits both hold for $Y$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The proof uses the stronger summable individual-projection criterion, proved locally by an exact martingale-coboundary series. No rho-mixing CLT is imported as a proof premise.

manifest_row.title: A rho-mixing CLT for square-integrable stationary sequences
manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\rho_Y(n)<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary real sequence, with one-sided coefficients $\rho_Y(n)$ from [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. There is a shift-invariant probability $Q$ on the coordinate sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^{\mathbb Z}$ such that its coordinate process $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ restricted to $k\ge0$ has the law of $Y$. The invertible left shift $T(x)_i=x_{i+1}$ preserves $Q$. Put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$ and $\mathcal G_k=\sigma(X_i:i\ge k)$. For every integer $k$, every $n\ge1$, and real square-integrable $U$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $V$ measurable in $\mathcal G_{k+n}$,
$$|\operatorname{Cov}_Q(U,V)|\le\rho_Y(n)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(U)\operatorname{Var}_Q(V)}.$$
If $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, then $T$ is ergodic: every event $A$ with $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$ has $Q(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be an invertible bimeasurable probability-preserving transformation on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ such that $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$ implies $Q(A)\in\{0,1\}$. Let $X_0\in L^2(Q)$ be real and centered, put $X_k=X_0\circ T^k$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$, and put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$. Suppose
$$\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]\|_2<\infty.$$
Then the $L^2$ series $H_0=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]$ converges. Put $H_k=H_0\circ T^k$ and $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$. The $D_k$ are stationary square-integrable martingale differences for $\mathcal F_k$, and for $n\ge1$,
$$S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k+H_0-H_n,\qquad \|H_0-H_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2.$$
With $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$,
$$S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2),$$
including $\tau^2=0$. If additionally $\sum_{j\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)|<\infty$, then
$$\tau^2=\mathbb E[X_0^2]+2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j).$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

subjects.source_mathematical_body_exact:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the centered strictly stationary square-integrable real sequence, and one of the three sufficient regimes.

[A1] AC is assumed for the bounded CLT, normal-law characteristic function and characteristic-function convergence criterion. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] A centered bounded stationary real sequence with summable strong-mixing coefficients has an absolutely summable covariance series and a CLT with its nonnegative covariance-sum variance, including variance zero. ([[thm-bounded-summable-strong-mixing-clt]])

[F2] Absolute tail quantiles have the original absolute-value law under uniform Lebesgue measure; square-integrable variables from fields with event coefficient $a$ satisfy $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^aQ_UQ_V$. ([[lem-strong-mixing-quantile-covariance-bound]])

[F3] A measurable scalar observation preserves strict stationarity and does not increase the strong-mixing coefficients. ([[lem-measurable-observation-does-not-increase-mixing-coefficients]])

[F4] Dominated convergence applies on arbitrary measure spaces and therefore also to absolutely dominated covariance series. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F5] Tonelli interchanges nonnegative product integrals, including integration against counting measure. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[F6] Holder's integral inequality holds for conjugate finite exponents on every measure space. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])

[F7] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds absolute product expectations of square-integrable real variables. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]])

[F8] Under AC the characteristic function of $N(0,s^2)$ is $e^{-s^2t^2/2}$, including $s=0$. ([[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]])

[F9] Under AC, weak convergence to a specified probability law is equivalent to pointwise convergence of characteristic functions to that of the law. ([[cor-characteristic-function-criterion-for-weak-convergence]])

[F10] Zero covariance-sum variance and absolute covariance summability give convergence of normalized sums in $L^2$ and in distribution to $N(0,0)$. ([[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]])

[F11] Variance and covariance are centered product expectations. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

[F12] The coefficient $\alpha_Y(n)$ is the event supremum for the past and the future separated by $n$. ([[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]])

## Proof

1.1 Write $Q=Q_{Y_0}$ for the absolute tail quantile in [F2], and put $w(u)=1+\sum_{r\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{u<\alpha_Y(r)\}}$ and $J=\int_0^1w(u)Q(u)^2\,du$. We first show in every stated regime that $J<\infty$ and $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. In regime 1, $Q\le B$ and [F5] give $J\le B^2(1+\sum_r\alpha_Y(r))<\infty$. This regime also already follows directly from [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 In regime 2 put $p=2+\delta$ and $\theta=1-2/p=\delta/(2+\delta)\in(0,1)$. Holder's inequality [F6] with exponents $p/2$ and $p/(p-2)$, followed by the quantile identity [F2], gives
$$\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta\left(\int_0^1Q(u)^p\,du\right)^{2/p}=\alpha_Y(r)^\theta(\mathbb E|Y_0|^p)^{2/p}.$$
Tonelli [F5] and the assumed summability yield $J<\infty$. Also $0\le\alpha_Y(r)\le1$ by its event definition, so $\alpha_Y(r)\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta$, proving unweighted summability. [F2, F5, F6, F12, step 1.1, given, algebra]

1.3 In regime 3, choose constants $C<\infty$ and $a\in(0,1)$ so $\alpha_Y(r)\le Ca^r$ outside a finite set of lags. Counting the positive integers satisfying $u<Ca^r$ shows $w(u)\le C_1+C_2\log(1/u)$ for $0<u<1$, with finite nonnegative constants $C_1,C_2$; also $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. The elementary inequality $xv\le x\log^+x+e^v$ for $x,v\ge0$ follows for $x>0$ by maximizing $xv-x\log x+x$ as a function of $x$, whose maximum is $e^v$; $x=0$ is immediate. Set $x=Q(u)^2$ and $v=\tfrac12\log(1/u)$, then integrate and use [F2]:
$$\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log(1/u)\,du\le2\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log^+(Q(u)^2)\,du+2\int_0^1u^{-1/2}\,du=4\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]+4<\infty.$$
Together with the assumed second moment this proves $J<\infty$. Thus the two properties announced in step 1.1 hold in all three regimes, without imposing a power moment in regime 3. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_r)$. By [F2], [F12] and [F5],
$$\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|\le4\sum_{r\ge1}\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du=4\int_0^1(w(u)-1)Q(u)^2\,du<\infty.$$
Set $D_Y=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|$. Expanding a finite centered sum over $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ and counting at most $|I|$ pairs at each positive lag gives $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Y_i)^2\le D_Y|I|$. For consecutive sums the exact expression is $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant and [F4] prove convergence to the stated $\sigma_Y^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of nonnegative variances. [F2, F4, F5, F11, F12, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 For an integer $M\ge1$ put $c_M(y)=\max(-M,\min(y,M))$, $Z_k^{(M)}=c_M(Y_k)-\mathbb Ec_M(Y_0)$, and $H_M(y)=y-c_M(y)$. Then $R_k^{(M)}=Y_k-Z_k^{(M)}=H_M(Y_k)-\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)$. Both processes are strictly stationary by [F3], and $Z^{(M)}$ is centered and bounded by $2M$. Its coefficients are bounded by $\alpha_Y$, whose sum is finite by steps 1.1–1.3. Thus [F1] gives an absolutely convergent covariance series with nonnegative sum $\sigma_M^2$, normalized variance convergence to $\sigma_M^2$, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_M^2)$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct]

2.3 Put $t_M=\mathbb P(|Y_0|>M)$ and let $Q_{H_M}$ be the absolute quantile of $H_M(Y_0)$. Since $|H_M(Y_0)|=(|Y_0|-M)_+\le|Y_0|$, monotonicity of tail probabilities gives $Q_{H_M}(u)\le Q(u)$, while $Q_{H_M}(u)=0$ for $u\ge t_M$ by its defining infimum. The centering in $R^{(M)}$ does not change any covariance, and $\operatorname{Var}(H_M(Y_0))\le\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)^2$. Applying [F2] to the raw, uncentered $H_M(Y_k)$, followed by [F5], therefore gives
$$D_{R^{(M)}}:=\mathbb E(R_0^{(M)})^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(R_0^{(M)},R_r^{(M)})|\le8\int_0^{t_M}w(u)Q(u)^2\,du=:e_M^2.$$
Here the integrand is integrable by steps 1.1–1.3, and $t_M\to0$ because $Y_0$ is finite almost surely; hence [F4] makes $e_M\to0$. The same finite covariance expansion as in step 2.1 now gives $\sup_n\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nR_k^{(M)}\|_2\le e_M$. This bound uses the raw remainder quantile, without asserting that the centered remainder has that quantile. [F2, F4, F5, F11, F12, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.1 The reverse triangle inequality for $L^2$ norms gives $|\|S_n/\sqrt n\|_2-\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\|_2|\le e_M$ by step 2.3. This norm inequality follows by expanding a square and applying [F7] to its mixed term. Using the variance limits in steps 2.1 and 2.2 yields $|\sigma_Y-\sigma_M|\le e_M$, where the square roots are nonnegative. Therefore $\sigma_M\to\sigma_Y$. [F7, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra]

3.2 For fixed real $t$, $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the unit-modulus derivative along the real interval, and [F7] give $|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-\mathbb Ee^{it\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}/\sqrt n}|\le |t|e_M$. By the CLT in step 2.2 and [F9], the second characteristic function tends to $e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}$, identified by [F8]. Consequently
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|\le |t|e_M+|e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|.$$
Let $M\to\infty$ and apply step 3.1. Under [A1], [F8]–[F9] prove $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$. The case $\sigma_Y^2=0$ is also independently supplied by [F10] using absolute covariance summability from step 2.1. All three regimes and the degenerate case follow. [A1, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎
