citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence, with $|Z_0|\le B$ almost surely for a finite $B$, and suppose
$$\sum_{r=1}^\infty\alpha_Z(r)<\infty.$$
Put $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$. Then its covariance series converges absolutely and
$$\sigma_Z^2=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r=1}^\infty\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(T_n)}n\ge0.$$
Moreover
$$T_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Z^2),$$
including $\sigma_Z^2=0$. Writing $D_Z=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)|$, every finite subset $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right)^2\le D_Z|I|.$$
The strong-mixing coefficient is that of [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, square-integrable real process ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and put $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$. If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$ and
$$\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k=0,$$
then $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nY_k\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in distribution to $N(0,0)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $Q=Q_{Y_0}$ for the absolute tail quantile in [F2], and put $w(u)=1+\sum_{r\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{u<\alpha_Y(r)\}}$ and $J=\int_0^1w(u)Q(u)^2\,du$. We first show in every stated regime that $J<\infty$ and $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. In regime 1, $Q\le B$ and [F5] give $J\le B^2(1+\sum_r\alpha_Y(r))<\infty$. This regime also already follows directly from [F1].

In regime 2 put $p=2+\delta$ and $\theta=1-2/p=\delta/(2+\delta)\in(0,1)$. Holder's inequality [F6] with exponents $p/2$ and $p/(p-2)$, followed by the quantile identity [F2], gives
$$\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta\left(\int_0^1Q(u)^p\,du\right)^{2/p}=\alpha_Y(r)^\theta(\mathbb E|Y_0|^p)^{2/p}.$$
Tonelli [F5] and the assumed summability yield $J<\infty$. Also $0\le\alpha_Y(r)\le1$ by its event definition, so $\alpha_Y(r)\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta$, proving unweighted summability.

In regime 3, choose constants $C<\infty$ and $a\in(0,1)$ so $\alpha_Y(r)\le Ca^r$ outside a finite set of lags. Counting the positive integers satisfying $u<Ca^r$ shows $w(u)\le C_1+C_2\log(1/u)$ for $0<u<1$, with finite nonnegative constants $C_1,C_2$; also $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. The elementary inequality $xv\le x\log^+x+e^v$ for $x,v\ge0$ follows for $x>0$ by maximizing $xv-x\log x+x$ as a function of $x$, whose maximum is $e^v$; $x=0$ is immediate. Set $x=Q(u)^2$ and $v=\tfrac12\log(1/u)$, then integrate and use [F2]:
$$\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log(1/u)\,du\le2\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log^+(Q(u)^2)\,du+2\int_0^1u^{-1/2}\,du=4\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]+4<\infty.$$
Together with the assumed second moment this proves $J<\infty$. Thus the two properties announced in step 1.1 hold in all three regimes, without imposing a power moment in regime 3.

Let $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_r)$. By [F2], [F12] and [F5],
$$\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|\le4\sum_{r\ge1}\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du=4\int_0^1(w(u)-1)Q(u)^2\,du<\infty.$$
Set $D_Y=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|$. Expanding a finite centered sum over $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ and counting at most $|I|$ pairs at each positive lag gives $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Y_i)^2\le D_Y|I|$. For consecutive sums the exact expression is $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant and [F4] prove convergence to the stated $\sigma_Y^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of nonnegative variances.

For an integer $M\ge1$ put $c_M(y)=\max(-M,\min(y,M))$, $Z_k^{(M)}=c_M(Y_k)-\mathbb Ec_M(Y_0)$, and $H_M(y)=y-c_M(y)$. Then $R_k^{(M)}=Y_k-Z_k^{(M)}=H_M(Y_k)-\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)$. Both processes are strictly stationary by [F3], and $Z^{(M)}$ is centered and bounded by $2M$. Its coefficients are bounded by $\alpha_Y$, whose sum is finite by steps 1.1–1.3. Thus [F1] gives an absolutely convergent covariance series with nonnegative sum $\sigma_M^2$, normalized variance convergence to $\sigma_M^2$, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_M^2)$.

Put $t_M=\mathbb P(|Y_0|>M)$ and let $Q_{H_M}$ be the absolute quantile of $H_M(Y_0)$. Since $|H_M(Y_0)|=(|Y_0|-M)_+\le|Y_0|$, monotonicity of tail probabilities gives $Q_{H_M}(u)\le Q(u)$, while $Q_{H_M}(u)=0$ for $u\ge t_M$ by its defining infimum. The centering in $R^{(M)}$ does not change any covariance, and $\operatorname{Var}(H_M(Y_0))\le\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)^2$. Applying [F2] to the raw, uncentered $H_M(Y_k)$, followed by [F5], therefore gives
$$D_{R^{(M)}}:=\mathbb E(R_0^{(M)})^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(R_0^{(M)},R_r^{(M)})|\le8\int_0^{t_M}w(u)Q(u)^2\,du=:e_M^2.$$
Here the integrand is integrable by steps 1.1–1.3, and $t_M\to0$ because $Y_0$ is finite almost surely; hence [F4] makes $e_M\to0$. The same finite covariance expansion as in step 2.1 now gives $\sup_n\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nR_k^{(M)}\|_2\le e_M$. This bound uses the raw remainder quantile, without asserting that the centered remainder has that quantile.

The reverse triangle inequality for $L^2$ norms gives $|\|S_n/\sqrt n\|_2-\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\|_2|\le e_M$ by step 2.3. This norm inequality follows by expanding a square and applying [F7] to its mixed term. Using the variance limits in steps 2.1 and 2.2 yields $|\sigma_Y-\sigma_M|\le e_M$, where the square roots are nonnegative. Therefore $\sigma_M\to\sigma_Y$.

For fixed real $t$, $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the unit-modulus derivative along the real interval, and [F7] give $|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-\mathbb Ee^{it\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}/\sqrt n}|\le |t|e_M$. By the CLT in step 2.2 and [F9], the second characteristic function tends to $e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}$, identified by [F8]. Consequently
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|\le |t|e_M+|e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|.$$
Let $M\to\infty$ and apply step 3.1. Under [A1], [F8]–[F9] prove $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$. The case $\sigma_Y^2=0$ is also independently supplied by [F10] using absolute covariance summability from step 2.1. All three regimes and the degenerate case follow.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 includes empty finite index sets; no CLT is asserted for an empty asymptotic sample sequence.
A zero observation gives Q=0, J=0 and all covariance sums zero. Step 2.3 includes t_M=0 with an empty integral and zero tail error.
The finite covariance expansion in step 2.1 includes n=1. Truncation is defined for every integer M>=1.
Step 3.2 covers sigma_Y=0 both through characteristic functions and the supplied degenerate-CLT lemma.
Step 1.2 uses delta>0, so both Holder exponents are finite and theta lies strictly between zero and one. Step 1.3 uses 0<a<1 and includes the convention at Y=0; no extra power moment is required.

AC is explicit in the Statement and A1 and used in steps 2.2 and 3.2 through bounded CLT, normal characteristic function and weak-convergence criterion. Truncations use the explicit integer sequence M.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the centered strictly stationary real sequence $Y$, finite second moment, and $\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty$.

[A1] AC is inherited through the rho-mixing CLT. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] The coefficient $\phi_Y(n)$ bounds $|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|$ for a positive-probability past event $A$ and an event $B$ in the separated future; $\rho_Y(n)$ is the supremum of their square-integrable variable correlations. ([[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]])

[F2] Real square-integrable random variables satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]])

[F3] Simple functions are dense in real $L^2$ on a probability space. ([[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]])

[F4] For a centered stationary real sequence of finite second moment, $\sum_{n\ge1}\rho_Y(n)<\infty$ gives absolute convergence and nonnegativity of the covariance variance, and the normal CLT with that variance, including zero. ([[thm-rho-mixing-clt-for-square-integrable-sequences]])

[F5] Variance and covariance are centered second and product moments. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

## Proof

1.1 Fix a gap $n\ge1$ and a split $k\ge0$, put $\mathcal A=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_k)$ and $\mathcal B=\sigma(Y_{k+n},Y_{k+n+1},\ldots)$, and put $\phi=\phi_Y(n)$. Take finite partitions $(A_i)$ in $\mathcal A$ and $(B_j)$ in $\mathcal B$. Write $a_i=\mathbb P(A_i)$, $b_j=\mathbb P(B_j)$, $p_{ij}=\mathbb P(A_i\cap B_j)$, and $d_{ij}=p_{ij}-a_ib_j$. For each fixed $i$ the $d_{ij}$ sum to zero. If $a_i>0$, their positive sum is $\mathbb P(A_i\cap B)-a_i\mathbb P(B)\le\phi a_i$ for $B=\bigcup_{j:d_{ij}>0}B_j$, by [F1]. Hence $\sum_j|d_{ij}|\le2\phi a_i$; when $a_i=0$, every $d_{ij}=0$ and the same bound holds. For each $j$, $|p_{ij}-a_ib_j|\le p_{ij}+a_ib_j$ gives $\sum_i|d_{ij}|\le2b_j$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For simple $U=\sum_i u_i\mathbf1_{A_i}$ and $V=\sum_j v_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$, [F5] and finite Cauchy–Schwarz with weights $|d_{ij}|$ give $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|=|\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}u_iv_j|\le(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|u_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|v_j^2)^{1/2}\le2\sqrt\phi\,\|U\|_2\|V\|_2$, using step 1.1's row and column bounds. The finite Cauchy–Schwarz inequality here is also the probability-space inequality [F2] on a finite set, after normalizing the total weight; if all weights vanish the conclusion is immediate. [F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For arbitrary real square-integrable $\mathcal A$-measurable $U$ and $\mathcal B$-measurable $V$, choose simple approximants in their respective $L^2$ spaces using [F3]. Their means, norms and product expectations converge by [F2]; therefore step 1.2's inequality passes to the limit. Apply it to $U-\mathbb EU$ and $V-\mathbb EV$ to get $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le2\sqrt\phi\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}$. Taking the supremum over positive-variance variables and then splits in [F1] proves $\rho_Y(n)\le2\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}$. No reversal of the conditioning direction of $\phi$ has been used. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

2.2 Summation of step 2.1 gives $\sum_{n\ge1}\rho_Y(n)\le2\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty$. The given stationarity, centering, and second-moment assumptions are exactly those of [F4], so that theorem proves absolute convergence and nonnegativity of the displayed covariance series and $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$ for positive or zero $\sigma_Y^2$. Thus every claimed conclusion holds. [A1, F4, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Source notes

The phi-to-rho bound is proved directly by finite partitions and $L^2$ approximation. The normal limit is supplied by the locally proved rho-mixing CLT, rather than an external uniform-mixing limit theorem.

If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Fix a gap $n\ge1$ and a split $k\ge0$, put $\mathcal A=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_k)$ and $\mathcal B=\sigma(Y_{k+n},Y_{k+n+1},\ldots)$, and put $\phi=\phi_Y(n)$. Take finite partitions $(A_i)$ in $\mathcal A$ and $(B_j)$ in $\mathcal B$. Write $a_i=\mathbb P(A_i)$, $b_j=\mathbb P(B_j)$, $p_{ij}=\mathbb P(A_i\cap B_j)$, and $d_{ij}=p_{ij}-a_ib_j$. For each fixed $i$ the $d_{ij}$ sum to zero. If $a_i>0$, their positive sum is $\mathbb P(A_i\cap B)-a_i\mathbb P(B)\le\phi a_i$ for $B=\bigcup_{j:d_{ij}>0}B_j$, by [F1]. Hence $\sum_j|d_{ij}|\le2\phi a_i$; when $a_i=0$, every $d_{ij}=0$ and the same bound holds. For each $j$, $|p_{ij}-a_ib_j|\le p_{ij}+a_ib_j$ gives $\sum_i|d_{ij}|\le2b_j$.

For simple $U=\sum_i u_i\mathbf1_{A_i}$ and $V=\sum_j v_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$, [F5] and finite Cauchy–Schwarz with weights $|d_{ij}|$ give $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|=|\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}u_iv_j|\le(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|u_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|v_j^2)^{1/2}\le2\sqrt\phi\,\|U\|_2\|V\|_2$, using step 1.1's row and column bounds. The finite Cauchy–Schwarz inequality here is also the probability-space inequality [F2] on a finite set, after normalizing the total weight; if all weights vanish the conclusion is immediate.

For arbitrary real square-integrable $\mathcal A$-measurable $U$ and $\mathcal B$-measurable $V$, choose simple approximants in their respective $L^2$ spaces using [F3]. Their means, norms and product expectations converge by [F2]; therefore step 1.2's inequality passes to the limit. Apply it to $U-\mathbb EU$ and $V-\mathbb EV$ to get $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le2\sqrt\phi\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}$. Taking the supremum over positive-variance variables and then splits in [F1] proves $\rho_Y(n)\le2\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}$. No reversal of the conditioning direction of $\phi$ has been used.

Summation of step 2.1 gives $\sum_{n\ge1}\rho_Y(n)\le2\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty$. The given stationarity, centering, and second-moment assumptions are exactly those of [F4], so that theorem proves absolute convergence and nonnegativity of the displayed covariance series and $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$ for positive or zero $\sigma_Y^2$. Thus every claimed conclusion holds.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a
$\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to $\phi$ ([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability
$\pi$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary
$P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose
shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. We take the
initial law to be $\pi$, which implies stationarity by
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]. Let
$f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$
be Borel with $\pi(f)=0$. Define
$\sigma_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$
only when the covariance series is absolutely convergent and the CLT is
established, as in
[[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Each of the following six conditions is sufficient for absolute convergence
of the covariance series and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the stationary Harris-ergodic chain and centered real function in the Statement, and any one of its six sufficient regimes.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed by the local probability, conditional-expectation and sequence-CLT suppliers. The Statement already includes this hypothesis.

[F1] [[lem-measurable-observation-does-not-increase-mixing-coefficients]] makes $Y_k=f(X_k)$ stationary and bounds each of its mixing coefficients by the corresponding chain coefficient.

[F2] [[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]] gives the pointwise polynomial total-variation bound with $\pi(M)<\infty$. [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]] gives the geometric bound with finite measurable envelope, or with bounded envelope in the uniform case.

[F3] The bounded-future Markov property and iterated-kernel identity are [[thm-markov-property-for-bounded-future-path-functionals]] and [[thm-chapman-kolmogorov-equations]]. The event-supremum convention is [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]], and known factors can be taken out using [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]].

[F4] [[thm-strong-mixing-clt-with-moment-conditions]] proves absolute covariance summability and the normal limit for bounded observations with summable alpha, for the stated $L^{2+\delta}$ alpha-summability condition, or for exponential alpha with the logarithmic moment.

[F5] [[lem-harris-geometric-ergodicity-has-integrable-rate-envelope]] supplies an integrable geometric envelope under the stated Harris, irreducibility and aperiodicity hypotheses. [[lem-geometric-total-variation-rate-controls-strong-mixing]] then bounds alpha by that geometric rate.

[F6] [[lem-geometric-reversible-chain-rho-mixing]] gives exponential rho for a stationary reversible geometrically ergodic chain under the stated recurrence hypotheses. [[thm-rho-mixing-clt-for-square-integrable-sequences]] proves the covariance-summable $L^2$ CLT when rho is summable.

[F7] [[lem-uniform-ergodicity-controls-uniform-mixing]] gives exponential phi under uniform ergodicity. [[thm-uniform-mixing-clt-for-square-integrable-sequences]] proves the covariance-summable $L^2$ CLT when the square roots of phi are summable.

[F8] [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] handles zero covariance long-run variance by a finite covariance expansion. [[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]] identifies the covariance sum only after absolute convergence and the CLT have been established.

[F9] [[thm-geometric-series]] proves convergence of $\sum_{j\ge0}q^j$ for every real $0\le q<1$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and any one of the six regimes in the Statement.

1.1 Put $Y_k=f(X_k)$. This is a centered stationary real sequence by [F1]. It is square-integrable in every case: boundedness suffices in case 1, the power moment suffices in cases 2 and 3 on the probability space, and cases 5 and 6 assume $L^2$. In case 4, split at $|f|=e$: on the bounded part $f^2\le e^2$, and on the other part $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$, so the stated logarithmic moment implies $L^2$. All sequence suppliers below therefore have their centering, stationarity and second-moment premises. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose a pointwise rate $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)a_n$ is available with $\pi(M)<\infty$. For any past event $A\in\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_j)$ and separated future event $B\in\sigma(X_{j+n},X_{j+n+1},\ldots)$, [F3] supplies $0\le h\le1$ with $E[\mathbf1_B\mid\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_j)]=P^nh(X_j)$ and $P(B)=\pi(h)$. Approximating $h$ uniformly by dyadic averages of its superlevel indicators gives $|P^nh(x)-\pi(h)|\le\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$: each indicator discrepancy is bounded by the defining event supremum. Consequently
$$|P(A\cap B)-P(A)P(B)|=|E[\mathbf1_A(P^nh(X_j)-\pi(h))]|\le\pi(M)a_n.$$
Taking the suprema and then applying [F1] gives $\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)a_n$. No measurability of an uncountable total-variation supremum is needed, because its measurable envelope bounds each event discrepancy pointwise. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 In case 1, take $a_n=n^{-m}$ in step 1.2. Since $m>1$, grouping $2^j\le n<2^{j+1}$ bounds each block of $\sum_n n^{-m}$ by $2^{-j(m-1)}$; [F9] makes the resulting geometric series finite. Thus $\sum_n\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$. The bounded branch of [F4] gives absolute covariance summability and the asserted normal limit for the normalized sums of $Y$. This uses the whole approved range $m>1$. [F2, F4, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 In case 2, put $\theta=\delta/(2+\delta)$. Step 1.2 gives $\alpha_Y(n)^\theta\le\pi(M)^\theta n^{-m\theta}$. The exact assumption $m\delta>2+\delta$ says $m\theta>1$, so the same dyadic argument and [F9] make these bounds summable. The power-moment branch of [F4] proves the same covariance and distribution conclusions. [F2, F4, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 In cases 3 and 4, [F5] replaces the possibly nonintegrable original envelope by a finite integrable geometric envelope with some rate $a\in(0,1)$. Thus $\alpha_Y(n)\le Ca^n$ by [F1] and [F5]. In case 3, every positive power of this bound is summable, so the $L^{2+\delta}$ branch of [F4] applies. In case 4, its exponential/logarithmic-moment branch applies directly. Each yields absolute covariance summability and the normal limit without strengthening the given moment assumption. [F1, F4, F5, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

4.1 In case 5, reversibility and the geometric-rate assumptions allow [F6] to give $\rho_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for some $r<1$. By [F1], $\rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n)$, so its series is summable. The $L^2$ rho-mixing theorem in [F6] proves the required covariance-summable CLT. [A1, F1, F6, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

4.2 In case 6, [F7] gives $\phi_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for some $r<1$. By [F1], $\sum_n\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}\le\sqrt C\sum_n r^{n/2}<\infty$. The uniform-mixing $L^2$ theorem in [F7] therefore gives the same conclusions. [A1, F1, F7, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

5.1 In all six cases the covariance series is absolutely convergent, its sum is finite and nonnegative, and the normalized sum converges to the centered normal with precisely that covariance sum. If the sum is zero, [F8] also proves the degenerate limit directly in $L^2$, so no division by an asymptotic variance is made. Stationarity makes $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}Y_k$ equal in law. The established limit is therefore exactly the displayed limit in the Statement, and only now does [F8] identify its variance as $\sigma_f^2$. [F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$. For $m>0$, say that $P$ has **polynomial total-variation rate of order $m$ with an integrable envelope** if there is a measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)n^{-m}\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

This is the specific envelope condition used with the polynomial-rate CLT cases on this page. It does not claim that every definition of polynomial ergodicity in the literature includes integrability of $M$.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant
probability $\pi$, and consider its stationary output process $X$. Assume it is $\phi$-irreducible ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose it is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]] and reversible with
respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense of
[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]. Then there are
$C<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that its maximal-correlation mixing
coefficient satisfies
$$\rho_X(n)\le Cr^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\rho_Y(n)<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. If for constants $C<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$
$$\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le Cr^n\quad(n\ge1),$$
then the uniform-mixing coefficient satisfies
$$\phi_X(n)\le Cr^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, square-integrable real process ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and put $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$. If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$ and
$$\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k=0,$$
then $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nY_k\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in distribution to $N(0,0)$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

In case 4, split at $|f|=e$: on the bounded part $f^2\le e^2$, and on the other part $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$, so the stated logarithmic moment implies $L^2$. Consequently

This uses the whole approved range $m>1$.

In case 2, put $\theta=\delta/(2+\delta)$. Step 1.2 gives $\alpha_Y(n)^\theta\le\pi(M)^\theta n^{-m\theta}$. The exact assumption $m\delta>2+\delta$ says $m\theta>1$, so the same dyadic argument and [F9] make these bounds summable. In cases 3 and 4, [F5] replaces the possibly nonintegrable original envelope by a finite integrable geometric envelope with some rate $a\in(0,1)$. Thus $\alpha_Y(n)\le Ca^n$ by [F1] and [F5]. In case 5, reversibility and the geometric-rate assumptions allow [F6] to give $\rho_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for some $r<1$. By [F1], $\rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n)$, so its series is summable. The $L^2$ rho-mixing theorem in [F6] proves the required covariance-summable CLT.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra generated by $\{\{f<q\}:q\in\mathbb Q\}$. Inductively, let $\mathcal A_{j+1}$ be the algebra generated by $\mathcal A_j$ and all sets $\{x:P(x,A)>q\}$ with $A\in\mathcal A_j$ and $q\in\mathbb Q$. These are subsets in $\mathcal F$ by [F1] and [F6]. Each algebra is countable: enumerate its generators and then all finite Boolean expressions in them. This also explicitly enumerates $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal A_j$. Put $\mathcal G=\sigma(\mathcal A)$. Since rational half-lines generate the real Borel sigma-field, $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable.

For $A\in\mathcal A$, all rational superlevel sets of $P(\cdot,A)$ belong to $\mathcal G$ by construction. The class $\mathcal D$ of $B\in\mathcal G$ for which $P(\cdot,B)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable contains $\mathcal A$ and $X$. It is closed under complements because $P(x,B^c)=1-P(x,B)$ and under countable disjoint unions because $P(x,\bigcup_lB_l)=\sum_lP(x,B_l)$ is a measurable increasing limit. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system, and [F2] gives $\mathcal D=\mathcal G$. The restriction $P_{\mathcal G}$ therefore is a probability kernel.

For every nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable $g$, integration against $P_{\mathcal G}(x,\cdot)$ agrees with integration against $P(x,\cdot)$: this holds for indicators by restriction, for nonnegative simple functions by finite additivity of the integral, and for general $g$ by [F7] and [F3]. Both integrals are allowed to be infinite. Induction in [F4], using this integration identity and step 1.2, gives $P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal G$, including $n=0$.

If $\pi$ is invariant, the same restriction identity for integrals gives $\int P_{\mathcal G}(x,B)(\pi|_{\mathcal G})(dx)=\int P(x,B)\pi(dx)=\pi(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal G$. This is invariance of $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ by [F5]. All generating enumerations in step 1.1 were explicit, so this construction introduces no choice assumption.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] choose an orthogonal matrix $O$ with $A=O\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)O^T$. By [F2], $Z=O^TU$ has independent standard-normal coordinates. Integration by parts in the density [F3], with $ze^{-z^2/2}\to0$ at both infinities, gives $EZ_i^2=1$. Every absolute moment of $V_i=Z_i^2-1$ is finite: for an integer $k\ge1$, $|z^2-1|^k\le(1+z^2)^k$, and this polynomial is integrable against $e^{-z^2/2}$. Thus $EV_i=0$, $E(U^TAU)=\sum_i\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}A$, and $U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i\lambda_iV_i$.

Expand the even power $(\sum_i\lambda_iV_i)^{2r}$ over ordered tuples of $2r$ indices. By [F4], a term whose tuple has an index appearing exactly once has expectation zero. Group all other terms by the partition of their $2r$ positions into equal-index blocks. Such a partition has block sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_q\ge2$ with $\sum_a k_a=2r$. For each fixed partition, taking absolute values and dropping the restriction that different blocks have distinct indices bounds its contribution by $\prod_{a=1}^q E|V_1|^{k_a}\prod_{a=1}^q\sum_i|\lambda_i|^{k_a}$. All these quantities are finite by step 1.1.

Put $L=(\sum_i\lambda_i^2)^{1/2}$. If $L=0$, the centered form is identically zero and the bound holds. Otherwise $|\lambda_i|/L\le1$ and $\sum_i(|\lambda_i|/L)^2=1$, so for every integer $k\ge2$, $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^k\le L^k$. Consequently each partition contribution in step 1.2 is bounded by $L^{2r}\prod_a E|V_1|^{k_a}$. There are finitely many partitions of the fixed set of $2r$ positions; the sum of these moment products over the partitions without singleton blocks is a finite constant $C_r$ depending only on $r$.

Since $2r$ is even, the expanded power is the absolute $2r$th power. Summing the bounds of step 2.1 therefore gives $E|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A|^{2r}\le C_r L^{2r}$. Finally $L^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^2$ by symmetry and orthogonal diagonalization. This proves the bound and the expectation assertion, including $A=0$, singular matrices and matrices of either sign.

$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC. If $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is finite convex and both $X$ and $\phi(X)$ are integrable, then $\phi(E[X\mid\mathcal G])\le E[\phi(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely; the left side is measurable and integrable.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: On real $L^2(\pi)$ put $Tf=Pf$ and $H=\{f:\pi(f)=0\}$. By [F3], conditional Jensen and stationarity give $\|Tf\|_2^2\le\pi(f^2)$ and $\pi(Tf)=\pi(f)$. These identities also show that the operator is well defined on almost-everywhere classes. Thus $T$ is a contraction preserving $H$, and $T1=1$. For bounded $f,g$, [F2] gives $\langle f,Tg\rangle=\langle Tf,g\rangle$ by integrating $f(x)g(y)$ against the flow measure. Bounded truncation converges in $L^2$ by [F5], so contraction and [F4] extend this symmetry to all $L^2$ functions. Iterated kernel integration agrees with $T^k$; for bounded functions this is [F7], and contraction extends the identity to $L^2$ classes.

For probability measures $\mu,
u$ and $0\le a\le1$, approximate $a$ uniformly by $2^{-q}\sum_{i=1}^{2^q}1_{\{a\ge i2^{-q}\}}$. Each indicator integral difference is bounded by the event-supremum TV distance, so $|\mu(a)-
u(a)|\le\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$ on taking limits. Applying this to $a=(h+\|h\|_\infty)/(2\|h\|_\infty)$ for nonzero bounded measurable $h$, and separating $h=0$, gives $|P^kh(x)-\pi(h)|\le2\|h\|_\infty M(x)r^k$.

Put $C_m=\{M\le m\}$ for positive integers $m$. If bounded $h$ vanishes off $C_m$ and $f=h-\pi(h)$, symmetry and invariance give $\|T^kf\|_2^2=\langle f,T^{2k}f\rangle=\int h(x)(P^{2k}h(x)-\pi(h))\,\pi(dx)$ for $k\ge1$. Step 1.2 therefore gives $0\le\|T^kf\|_2^2\le2m\|h\|_\infty^2r^{2k}$. Write $A=\sqrt{2m}\|h\|_\infty<\infty$, so $\|T^kf\|_2\le Ar^k$. No integral of $M$ over the whole state space has been used.

For $u\in H$ and $a\ge1$, symmetry and [F4] give $\|T^au\|_2^2=\langle u,T^{2a}u\rangle\le\|u\|_2\|T^{2a}u\|_2$. Repeating with $a=1,2,4,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}$ yields $\|Tu\|_2\le\|u\|_2^{1-2^{-\ell}}\|T^{2^\ell}u\|_2^{2^{-\ell}}$. For the $f$ in step 2.1, if $f=0$ the bound $\|Tf\|_2\le r\|f\|_2$ is immediate; otherwise $A>0$ and the last display is at most $rA^{2^{-\ell}}\|f\|_2^{1-2^{-\ell}}$, tending to $r\|f\|_2$. Hence that bound holds for every such $f$.

For $u\in H$ choose a finite measurable representative and put $h_m=1_{C_m}\max(-m,\min(u,m))$. Finiteness of $M$ gives $h_m\to u$ almost everywhere and $|h_m-u|\le|u|$, so [F5] gives $h_m\to u$ in $L^2$. By [F4], $\pi(h_m)\to0$, and therefore $h_m-\pi(h_m)\to u$ in $L^2$. Applying step 2.2 to these centered functions and taking limits through the contraction $T$ gives $\|Tu\|_2\le r\|u\|_2$. Iteration on $H$ proves $\|T^nu\|_2\le r^n\|u\|_2$ for all $n\ge1$. This also covers $H=\{0\}$.

Fix $j\ge0$ and bounded centered real $U,V$ measurable respectively for $\mathcal F_j$ and $\sigma(X_{j+n},X_{j+n+1},\ldots)$. By [F6] there is bounded measurable $g$ such that $E[V\mid\mathcal F_{j+n}]=g(X_{j+n})$. Stationarity and [F9] give $\pi(g)=0$ and $\|g\|_2\le\|V\|_2$. The tower property and [F7] give $E[V\mid\mathcal F_j]=P^ng(X_j)$. Taking out $U$, applying [F4] and stationarity, and then step 2.3, yields $|E[UV]|=|E[UP^ng(X_j)]|\le\|U\|_2\|T^ng\|_2\le r^n\|U\|_2\|V\|_2$.

For general centered square-integrable $U,V$ in the same sigma-algebras, truncate each at levels $\pm m$ and subtract its expectation. By [F5] and [F4], these bounded centered variables converge in $L^2$; [F4] passes their covariances and norms to the limit in step 3.1. Dividing by the positive standard deviations and taking the suprema in [F10] proves $\rho_X(n)\le r^n$. If no positive-variance variables exist, the coefficient is zero by the nonnegative empty-supremum convention. Thus the stated conclusion holds with $C=1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
The sum of a complex power series is analytic on its open disc of convergence.
Every function analytic on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ is holomorphic on $U$.

If $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ has radius $R$, then for every $k\in\mathbb N$ and $|z-a|<R$,
$$f^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{n\ge k}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}c_n(z-a)^{n-k}.$$
Every derived series has radius $R$.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, let $0<r<R$, and let $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. Define $f^{(0)}=f$ and, whenever it exists, $f^{(n+1)}=(f^{(n)})'$. Then every $f^{(n)}$ exists on $D(a,r)$ and, for every $z\in D(a,r)$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)^{n+1}}\,d\zeta.$$

In particular, every holomorphic function has complex derivatives of all orders locally.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, let $0<r<R$, and suppose $M\ge0$ satisfies $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ whenever $|\zeta-a|=r$. If $c_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!$ is the $n$th coefficient of the Taylor series of $f$ at $a$, then

$$|c_n|\le\frac{M}{r^n}\qquad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

If $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ on $|\zeta-a|=r$, then the $n$th Taylor coefficient $c_n$ satisfies $|c_n|\le M/r^n$.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim:
Set $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. On $\widetilde X=X	imes\{0,1\}$ define $K_{x,1}=
u$; define $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon
u)/(1-\epsilon)$ for $x\in C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ otherwise. The split kernel is
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),B	imes\{j\})=\int_B w_j(y)K_{x,i}(dy).$$
Nonnegativity follows from [F1], measurability from [F3], and finite summation over the two flag sections defines a probability on every product-measurable event. Thus [F2] realizes the split path. If the initial flag at $x$ has probabilities $w_i(x)$, summing it gives $\sum_iw_i(x)K_{x,i}=Q(x,\cdot)$. The same summation at each subsequent time shows that the $x$-coordinate path has the original $Q$-chain law. The set $\alpha=C	imes\{1\}$ is an atom: all its states have the identical outgoing transition obtained by using $
u$.

Put $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Summing its incoming transitions first over $i$ gives $\pi Q=\pi$ and then assigns the new flag according to $w_j$, proving $\widetilde\pi\widetilde Q=\widetilde\pi$ by [F13]. Let $p=\widetilde\pi(\alpha)=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$, and let $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$, an ordinary normalized restriction. Write $\mathbb P_\alpha=\mathbb P_\kappa$; its future after time zero is the same from every atom state. Starting in $\alpha$, the next coordinate law is $\nu$ and subsequent coordinate transitions are $Q$, so
$$u_0=1,\qquad u_n=\mathbb P_\alpha(Z_n\in\alpha)=\epsilon\nu Q^{n-1}(C)\quad(n\ge1).$$
The hypothesis implies $|u_n-p|\le c\theta^n$ for all $n\ge0$ after increasing a finite $c$.

Let $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$ and $f_n=\mathbb P_\alpha(\tau=n)$ for $n\ge1$, with $f_0=0$. Decompose a visit at time $n\ge1$ by the first return time and use [F4] and the common atom transition to obtain $u_n=\sum_{j=1}^nf_ju_{n-j}$. The possible event $\tau=\infty$ contributes zero. For $|z|<1$, absolute convergence and [F8] give
$$U(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}u_nz^n=\frac1{1-F(z)},\qquad F(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}f_nz^n.$$
Here $|F(z)|\le|z|\sum_nf_n\le|z|<1$, so the denominator is legitimate. Since $u_n-p$ decays geometrically, [F9] gives $U(z)=p/(1-z)+J(z)$ with $J$ holomorphic on $|z|<\theta^{-1}$. For real $t\uparrow1$, $U(t)\to\infty$; hence $F(t)\to1$ and [F7] gives $\sum_nf_n=1$.

Near $z=1$ the expression
$$\widehat F(z)=1-\frac{1-z}{p+(1-z)J(z)}$$
is holomorphic and agrees with $F$ on its overlap with $|z|<1$. Indeed the denominator has value $p>0$ at $1$ and remains nonzero on a sufficiently small disk; the quotient is complex differentiable there by the difference-quotient formula for the derivative of a reciprocal. By [F10], for $0<t<1$ and $k\ge0$, $F^{(k)}(t)=\sum_{n\ge k}f_n(n)_kt^{n-k}$, where $(n)_k=n!/(n-k)!$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ and using [F7] and derivative continuity from [F11] gives $\sum_{n\ge k}f_n(n)_k=\widehat F^{(k)}(1)$. Choose a radius $\delta>0$ whose closed disk about $1$ lies strictly within this holomorphic neighborhood and a finite bound $B$ for $|\widehat F|$ on its circle. [F12] then bounds these nonnegative derivative values by $k!B\delta^{-k}$.

For $0<h<\delta$, the finite binomial expansion for each integer $n$, followed by [F8], yields
$$\mathbb E_\alpha[(1+h)^\tau]=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{h^k}{k!}\sum_{n\ge k}f_n(n)_k\le\frac{B}{1-h/\delta}<\infty.$$
Thus some $b>1$ has $\mathbb E_\alpha b^\tau<\infty$. The return is almost surely finite by step 2.1. This argument establishes an exponential moment from positivity and analytic continuation; it does not assume in advance that the original series $F$ converges beyond the unit disk.

Let $T=\inf\{n\ge0:Z_n\in\alpha\}$ and start the split chain from $\widetilde\pi$. By [F6], $I_j=1_\alpha(Z_j)$ have mean $p$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(I_0,I_n)=p(u_n-p)$. Expanding the square of $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}I_j-p$ and summing the geometric covariance bound from step 1.2 gives expectation at most $c_1/N$ for some finite $c_1$. On $\{T\ge N\}$ this square equals $p^2$, so $\mathbb P_{\widetilde\pi}(T\ge N)\le c_1/(Np^2)\to0$. In particular the stationary split chain hits the atom almost surely; no unproved Harris or skeleton-recurrence theorem is needed.

For bounded nonnegative $g$, decompose $g(Z_N)$ by the last atom visit at times $0,\ldots,N$. A last visit at time $N-k$ contributes $p\mathbb E_\alpha[g(Z_k);\tau>k]$, by stationarity and [F5]. The remaining paths have no atom visit through time $N$, and their contribution $R_N$ lies between zero and $\|g\|_\infty\mathbb P_{\widetilde\pi}(T>N)$. Thus
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\sum_{k=0}^N\mathbb E_\alpha[g(Z_k);\tau>k]+R_N.$$
Let $N\to\infty$ using step 3.1, then extend from bounded $g$ to all nonnegative measurable $g$ using [F7] and [F8]. This proves the stationary occupation identity $\widetilde\pi(g)=p\mathbb E_\alpha\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k)$. At $k=0$ the atom state has law $\kappa$; subsequent transitions are independent of which atom state was chosen, so this argument does not require $g$ to be constant on $\alpha$.

Fix $1<s<b$ and let $g(z)=\mathbb E_zs^T$, allowing infinity. The bounded path functions $s^{T\wedge l}$ increase to $s^T$, so [F5] and [F7] give measurability and the Markov identity for this nonnegative function by truncation. On $\alpha$, $g=1$. For $k\ge1$, on $\{\tau>k\}$, the residual time to $\alpha$ is $\tau-k$; the Markov identity and step 3.2 give
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\left(1+\mathbb E_\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{\tau-1}s^{\tau-k}\right)\le p\mathbb E_\alpha[\tau s^\tau]<\infty.$$
The last moment is finite because $\sup_{j\ge1}j(s/b)^j<\infty$ and step 2.3 bounds $\mathbb E_\alpha b^\tau$. For the coordinate chain initialized with the prescribed flag, its first $C$ visit $\sigma_C$ is no later than its first atom visit $T$. Consequently $H(x)=\mathbb E_xs^{\sigma_C}$ is measurable by the same bounded-path approximation and $\pi(H)\le\widetilde\pi(g)<\infty$. This proves the conclusion, including the null-set qualification.
