Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim: For a finite real $U$, write $T(t)=\mathbb P(|U|>t)$ for $t\ge0$. The tail tends to zero at infinity, is nonincreasing and is right-continuous. Thus $Q_U(u)$ is finite for $u>0$, is nonincreasing, and is Borel measurable. More precisely, $Q_U(u)>t$ if and only if $u<T(t)$: if $T(t)\le u$, then $t$ belongs to the set defining the infimum; if $T(t)>u$, right-continuity supplies an $\varepsilon>0$ with $T(t+\varepsilon)>u$, so that infimum exceeds $t$. Consequently Lebesgue measure on $(0,1)$ gives $\lambda\{u:Q_U(u)>t\}=T(t)$ for every $t\ge0$. The laws of $Q_U$ under $\lambda$ and of $|U|$ therefore agree on all closed left rays and both have total mass one. These rays form a pi-system and generate the Borel sigma-algebra: their differences give half-open intervals, and countable unions of those give all open intervals. By [F6] the laws agree, proving the stated integral identity. In particular $\int_0^1Q_U^2=\mathbb EU^2$.

Suppose first $U,V\ge0$ and $U,V\in L^2$. Their first moments and $\mathbb E(UV)$ are finite by [F3]. The threshold-indicator identities and [F5] give $\mathbb E(UV)=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s,V>t)\,ds\,dt$ and $\mathbb EU\mathbb EV=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s)\mathbb P(V>t)\,ds\,dt$. Both integrands have finite integrals, so their difference represents the covariance and the integral triangle inequality applies. The absolute threshold-indicator covariance is bounded by $a$, by $\mathbb P(U>s)$, and by $\mathbb P(V>t)$, since the joint probability and the product probability both lie between zero and either marginal probability.

Put $T_U(s)=\mathbb P(U>s)$ and $T_V(t)=\mathbb P(V>t)$. By [F5] and step 1.1,
$$\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\min\{a,T_U(s),T_V(t)\}\,ds\,dt=\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
Indeed the minimum is $\int_0^a\mathbf1_{\{u<T_U(s)\}}\mathbf1_{\{u<T_V(t)\}}\,du$, and each inner threshold set has length its quantile. The right-hand side is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz on $(0,1)$ and the squared-quantile identity in step 1.1; this particular integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by integrating $(Q_U-cQ_V)^2\ge0$ and minimizing the resulting quadratic, with the zero-norm case immediate. Step 1.2 therefore proves the covariance bound with constant one for nonnegative $U,V$.

For real $U,V$, expand $\operatorname{Cov}(U^+-U^-,V^+-V^-)$ into four terms. Each nonnegative part has a tail quantile at most the corresponding absolute quantile, because its tail probabilities are smaller. The result of step 1.3 bounds each term by $\int_0^aQ_UQ_V$; the triangle inequality gives the asserted factor four. If $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$, their absolute quantiles are bounded by $A,B$, so the bound becomes $4ABa$, including $a=0$ or either zero bound.

For complex $U,V$, expand $\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV$ into the four real bilinear covariance terms of their real and imaginary parts. Each real part is bounded in absolute value by $A$ or $B$, so step 2.1 and the complex triangle inequality give $16ABa$. Finally, for observations separated by $n$, both collection sigma-algebras are sub-sigma-algebras of the past and future fields appearing in [F1]; their event supremum is therefore at most $\alpha_Y(n)$. All assertions follow.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then
every element of $L^p(\mu)$ can be approximated in $L^p$ by simple functions
whose supports have finite measure.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: For finite $F\subset\mathbb Z$, choose an integer $m\ge0$ with $F+m\subset\mathbb N_0$ and prescribe the law of $(X_i)_{i\in F}$ to be that of $(Y_{i+m})_{i\in F}$. If $m'$ is another permissible shift, stationarity compares the smaller shift with the larger one, so the law is independent of the choice. Restrictions are consistent because finitely many coordinate sets can be translated by one common shift. Every coordinate space is the standard Borel space $\mathbb R$, so [F1] gives $Q$. Its nonnegative restriction equals the process law of $Y$ on cylinders and hence everywhere by [F5]. Translating finite sets does not change their prescribed laws, so $Q\circ T^{-1}=Q$ by the same uniqueness argument. Both $T$ and its inverse are measurable because their coordinate maps are coordinates.

For any subset $I\subset\mathbb Z$, let $\mathcal A_I$ be the algebra of events depending on finitely many coordinates in $I$. Every event in $\sigma(X_i:i\in I)$ can be approximated in symmetric-difference probability by $\mathcal A_I$. Indeed, the approximable events are closed under complements. For a countable union, first replace that union by a finite subunion with arbitrarily small lost probability, using continuity from below, then approximate its finitely many constituent events and apply the union bound. Thus the approximable events form a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal A_I$. By [F4], approximate an $L^2$ variable by simple functions, and approximate the finitely many indicator events of each simple function by $\mathcal A_I$ events. For an indicator the squared $L^2$ error is its symmetric-difference probability; finite summation gives the required arbitrarily small $L^2$ error for a simple function. Consequently every such variable has finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants.

First suppose $U$ and $V$ depend on finitely many coordinates in $(-\infty,k]$ and $[k+n,\infty)$, respectively. Translate all coordinates by one integer $m\ge0$ so that the used past coordinates and the split $k+m$ are nonnegative. Their joint distribution is an original-process distribution by step 1.1. The translated variables are measurable in $\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{k+m})$ and $\sigma(Y_{k+m+n},Y_{k+m+n+1},\ldots)$, so [F2] proves the asserted covariance inequality when both variances are positive. A variable of variance zero equals its mean almost surely and has zero covariance, so the inequality holds then too. For arbitrary $U,V$, take step 1.2's finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants. Their means, second moments, and covariances converge by [F3], so passage to the limit proves the same inequality.

Assume $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, and let $A$ satisfy $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$, with $p=Q(A)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, step 1.2 supplies a finite-coordinate event $C$ with $Q(A\mathbin\triangle C)<\varepsilon$; enlarge its coordinate support to $[-m,m]$ for some $m\ge0$. For $n>2m$, $C$ is in $\mathcal F_m$ and $T^{-n}C$ is in $\mathcal G_{n-m}$. Step 2.1 applied to their indicators gives $|Q(C\cap T^{-n}C)-Q(C)^2|\le\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$, since every indicator variance is at most $1/4$. Invariance modulo null sets and measure preservation imply $Q(A\cap T^{-n}A)=p$. The intersection changes in probability by at most $2\varepsilon$ upon replacing both copies of $A$ by copies of $C$, and $|p^2-Q(C)^2|\le2\varepsilon$. Hence $|p-p^2|\le4\varepsilon+\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$. Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain $p=p^2$. Therefore $p\in\{0,1\}$, proving [F6] and the stronger mod-null formulation claimed.

Composition with $T^k$ is an $L^2$ isometry, so step 1.1 yields $H_k=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_k]$ in $L^2$, with $H_k$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $\|H_k\|_2=\|H_0\|_2$. Representatives may be fixed for the countably many indices; discard a countable union of null sets for their identities.

By [F1], conditional expectation is continuous in $L^2$. Apply [F2]'s tower property to the partial sums in step 1.2 and pass to the $L^2$ limit to obtain $\mathbb E[H_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=H_{k-1}-\mathbb E[X_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$. Thus $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$ is square-integrable and $\mathcal F_k$ measurable, with $\mathbb E[D_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=0$. Also $D_k=D_1\circ T^{k-1}$, so the differences are stationary. Summing their defining identity gives $S_n=M_n+R_n$, where $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$, $R_n=H_0-H_n$, and $\|R_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2$. In particular $R_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability by [F8].

Put $q_0=\mathbb E[D_1^2\mid\mathcal F_0]$. It is nonnegative, integrable, and has expectation $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$ by [F1]. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=q_0\circ T^{k-1}$. The map $\omega\mapsto(q_0(T^j\omega))_{j\ge0}$ intertwines $T$ with the canonical one-sided shift. Hence a shift-invariant event for this process pulls back to a $T$-invariant event modulo null sets, whose probability is zero or one by the assumed ergodicity. The process is stationary, integrable and ergodic, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\to\tau^2$ almost surely. The limiting variance is therefore a constant.

If $\tau^2>0$, let $Z_{n,k}=D_k/(\tau\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$, and let $Z_{n,k}=0$ for $k>n$; use the filtration $\mathcal F_{n,k}=\mathcal F_{\min(k,n)}$ for $k\ge0$. Step 1.3 makes each row a square-integrable martingale-difference row. The row sums and clocks are eventually constant, and step 2.1 shows their terminal clocks converge almost surely to $1$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity gives $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\tau\sqrt n\}}]\to0$ by [F7]. Thus [F6] gives $M_n/(\tau\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Scaling and the perturbation in step 1.3 give $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ by [F8].

If $\tau^2=0$, stationarity implies $\mathbb E[D_k^2]=0$ for every $k$, so $M_n=0$ almost surely. Step 1.3 gives $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability. The constant sequence $0$ has weak limit the point mass $N(0,0)$; [F8] transfers that limit to $S_n/\sqrt n$. This establishes the asserted CLT in both variance cases.

Suppose the additional covariance summability holds, and put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-j/n)\gamma_j\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j$, by [F7] on counting measure with summable dominator $|\gamma_j|$. For $i<j$, $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$ measurable, so [F2], [F4], and step 1.3 give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E[M_n^2]=n\tau^2$. The identity $S_n=M_n+R_n$ and [F4] imply $|\mathbb E[S_n^2]-n\tau^2|/n\le\|R_n\|_2^2/n+2\|R_n\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$, since $\|R_n\|_2$ is bounded. All $S_n$ are centered, so [F9] identifies the two variance limits and proves the stated covariance formula, including $\tau^2=0$.

Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. There is a countably generated sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ such that $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $P$, restricted to events in $\mathcal G$, is a probability kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$ on $(X,\mathcal G)$. For every $n\ge0$, $x\in X$, and $B\in\mathcal G$,
$$P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B).$$
If $\pi$ is invariant for $P$, then $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ is invariant for $P_{\mathcal G}$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel, and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Apply [F2] to $M_0$ to obtain a countably generated $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal X$, the restricted kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$, and invariant probability $\pi_{\mathcal G}=\pi|_{\mathcal G}$. Thus $P_{\mathcal G}$ is $\pi_{\mathcal G}$-irreducible by [F7]. Applying [F3] on this countably generated space gives an $m\ge1$, a $D\in\mathcal G$ with $\pi(D)>0$, a probability $
u_0$ on $\mathcal G$ with $
u_0(D)>0$, and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $P_{\mathcal G}^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon_0
u_0$ on $D$. No small-set assertion on the original sigma-field is being made.

Since $M_0$ is finite everywhere, $D\cap\{M_0\le K\}$ increases to $D$ as the positive integer $K$ increases. Choose $K$ so $C=D\cap\{M_0\le K\}$ has both $\pi(C)>0$ and $
u_0(C)>0$. Choose a finite integer $L\ge K$ and put $a=
u_0(M_0\le L)>0$, $
u(B)=
u_0(B\cap\{M_0\le L\})/a$. Choose $0<\epsilon<\min(1,\epsilon_0a)$. For $Q=P_{\mathcal G}^m$ this gives $Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u$ on $C$, $
u(M_0)\le L$, and $M_0\le K$ on $C$.

For $n\ge1$, the restricted-iteration identity in [F2] and [F1] give
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le\int M_0(x)r_0^{mn}\nu(dx)\le L(r_0^m)^n.$$
For $n=0$ the absolute difference is at most $1$. Therefore [F4] applies with constant $\max(1,L)$ and rate $r_0^m$. It supplies $s>1$ and a measurable $H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^\sigma]$, where $\sigma=\inf\{j\ge0:X_{jm}\in C\}$, such that $\pi(H)<\infty$. Indeed the skeleton path restricted to $\mathcal G$ under the full canonical $P$-chain has the $Q$-chain law: its finite-dimensional cylinder probabilities agree by the iterated-kernel identity in [F2]. Thus the same $H$ is the entrance-time moment for the original chain of [F5].

Choose $\max(r_0,s^{-1/m})<r_1<1$, and set $S=m\sigma$ and $K_1=\max(1,K)$. Fix $A\in\mathcal X$ and $n\ge1$. On $\{S\le n\}$, decompose into the finitely many events $\{S=j\}$ and use [F6] to replace the conditional terminal indicator by $P^{n-j}(X_j,A)$. Since $X_j\in C$, [F1] bounds its difference from $\pi(A)$ by $K_1r_0^{n-j}$; when $j=n$, use $|1_A(X_n)-\pi(A)|\le1\le K_1$. On $\{S>n\}$ use the bound $1$. Subtracting $\pi(A)$ on these two events gives
$$|P^n(x,A)-\pi(A)|\le\mathbb P_x(S>n)+K_1\mathbb E_x[r_0^{n-S};S\le n]\le(1+K_1)r_1^nH(x).$$
For the final inequality, $r_1^{-S}\le s^\sigma$, and on $S\le n$ one has $r_0^{n-S}\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$; on $S>n$, $1\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$. This argument is for each original measurable event $A$, so taking its supremum controls the full original total variation and does not require measurability of a total-variation supremum.

The measurable set $N=\{H=\infty\}$ is $\pi$-null by step 2.1. Define $M_1(x)=(1+K_1)H(x)$ for $x\notin N$ and $M_1(x)=M_0(x)$ for $x\in N$. It is measurable and finite everywhere, and $\pi(M_1)<\infty$. Off $N$, step 2.2 gives the desired bound with rate $r_1$; on $N$, [F1] gives it because $r_0<r_1$. Taking $M=M_1$ and $r=r_1$ proves the full Statement. AC was used precisely through [F3] and the path-space and Markov suppliers [F4]–[F6].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume AC. For every positive integer $r$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, depending only on $r$, such that for every integer $n\ge1$, independent standard-normal variables $U_1,\ldots,U_n$, and real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $A$,
$$E\left|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^{2r}\le C_r\left(\sum_{i,k=1}^n A_{ik}^2\right)^r.$$
In particular $E(U^TAU)=\operatorname{tr}A$. The matrix may be singular or indefinite.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $\mathbb EX=0$ and $\mathbb EX^2=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $\varphi_X(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2)$ as $t\to0$. No third moment or choice axiom is assumed. The same scalar estimates give $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ for every real u. More precisely, for $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, $$|r(u)|\le \min(|u|^3/3,4u^2),\qquad |e^{iu}-1-iu|\le u^2.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)$. By [F1]–[F2], $|\gamma_r|\le4B^2\alpha_Z(r)$ for $r\ge1$, so $D_Z<\infty$. Expanding the square of a sum indexed by a finite subset $I$ gives its diagonal terms $|I|\gamma_0$ and off-diagonal terms $2\gamma_{j-i}$ for pairs $i<j$ in $I$. For each fixed positive lag there are at most $|I|$ such pairs. Thus the asserted bound $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i)^2\le D_Z|I|$ holds, also for $I=\varnothing$. For a consecutive block, the same expansion gives $\operatorname{Var}(T_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant $2|\gamma_r|$ and [F4] imply convergence to the stated $\sigma_Z^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of variances.

Extend the coefficient convention by $\alpha_Z(0)=1$. It is nonincreasing: increasing the separation restricts the future sigma-algebra in [F1]. For ordered indices $i\le j\le k\le l$, write $a=j-i$ and $c=l-k$. If $a>0$, centering of $Z_i$ and [F2] applied to $Z_i$ and $Z_jZ_kZ_l$ give $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(a)$; if $a=0$, the trivial bound $B^4$ suffices. Splitting off the centered last factor gives the same bound with $c$. Therefore $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(\max(a,c))$. There are at most $24$ orderings, at most $p$ choices each for the first index and the middle gap, and $2r+1$ pairs $(a,c)$ with maximum $r$. Hence
$$\mathbb ET_p^4\le96B^4p^2\sum_{r=0}^p(2r+1)\alpha_Z(r)=o(p^3).$$
To justify the last limit, for each fixed $R$, $p^{-1}\sum_{r\le R}r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, whereas $p^{-1}\sum_{R<r\le p}r\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{r>R}\alpha_Z(r)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$; the unweighted part divided by $p$ also tends to zero. Repeated indices are included by the convention at zero.

Set $\varepsilon_p=\mathbb ET_p^4/p^3$ and $\eta_n=\sup_{p\ge\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor}\varepsilon_p$. By step 1.2, $\eta_n\to0$. For sufficiently large $n$, define $h_n=\min(n^{1/8},\eta_n^{-1/4})$, interpreting the second entry as $+\infty$ if $\eta_n=0$, and ignore the finitely many earlier $n$. Then $h_n\to\infty$, $h_n=o(n^{1/4})$, and $h_n^2\eta_n\to0$. Put $p_n=\lceil\sqrt n h_n\rceil$, $q_n=\lfloor\sqrt n/h_n\rfloor$, and $k_n=\lfloor n/(p_n+q_n)\rfloor$. Thus $p_n,q_n\to\infty$, $p_n/n\to0$, $q_n/p_n\to0$, and $k_np_n/n\to1$. Retain $k_n$ consecutive blocks of length $p_n$, separated by discarded blocks of length $q_n$, and discard the final remainder. Their discarded index set $I_n$ has cardinality at most $k_nq_n+p_n+q_n=o(n)$. Step 1.1 gives $\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in I_n}Z_i\|_2^2\le D_Z|I_n|/n\to0$, controlling all gaps together without asserting their independence.

Summability and monotonicity imply $r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, since $\lfloor r/2\rfloor\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor}^r\alpha_Z(s)$. For large $n$, $n/p_n\le\sqrt n/h_n\le2q_n$, so $k_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\le2q_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\to0$. Let $B_{n,j}$ denote the sum in retained block $j$. At a fixed real frequency $t$, put $U_j=e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}$. Both each factor and every partial product have modulus at most one. The partial product through block $j$ is measurable before the gap preceding block $j+1$, so [F2] bounds the discrepancy in factoring its expectation from $U_{j+1}$ by $16\alpha_Z(q_n)$. Telescoping these factorizations gives
$$\left|\mathbb E e^{it\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}B_{n,j}/\sqrt n}-\prod_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}\right|\le16(k_n-1)\alpha_Z(q_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
This compares characteristic functions only and requires no independent copies or coupling construction.

Write $W_{n,j}=B_{n,j}/\sqrt n$. These variables are centered and each has the law of $T_{p_n}/\sqrt n$ by stationarity. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 imply $\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2=(k_np_n/n)\operatorname{Var}(T_{p_n})/p_n\to\sigma_Z^2$. Also
$$\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4=\frac{k_n\mathbb ET_{p_n}^4}{n^2}\le\frac{p_n^2}{n}\varepsilon_{p_n}\longrightarrow0,$$
because $p_n^2/n=O(h_n^2)$ and $\varepsilon_{p_n}\le\eta_n$. For every $\delta>0$, the Lindeberg sum of these block marginals is at most $\delta^{-2}\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4\to0$. Applying [F5] first to $|W|,W^2$ and then the finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields $\sum_j\mathbb E|W_{n,j}|^3\le(\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2)^{1/2}(\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4)^{1/2}\to0$. Finally $\max_j(\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2)^2\le\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4\to0$. No uniform-integrability hypothesis or deterministic block bound tending to zero has been assumed.

For fixed $t$, [F6] gives $\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}=1-a_{n,j}+r_{n,j}$, where $a_{n,j}=t^2\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2/2\ge0$ and $\sum_j|r_{n,j}|\le |t|^3\sum_j\mathbb E|W_{n,j}|^3/3\to0$. Step 3.1 gives $\sum_ja_{n,j}\to t^2\sigma_Z^2/2$ and $\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\le(\max_ja_{n,j})\sum_ja_{n,j}\to0$. The elementary real Taylor bound $|1-a-e^{-a}|\le a^2/2$ for $a\ge0$ follows by integrating the second derivative $e^{-a}\le1$ twice. Since both $|\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}|$ and $e^{-a_{n,j}}$ are at most one, the product telescoping inequality now gives
$$\left|\prod_j\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}-e^{-\sum_ja_{n,j}}\right|\le\sum_j|r_{n,j}|+\frac12\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\longrightarrow0.$$
Thus the product characteristic function tends to $e^{-t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}$.

The discarded normalized sum in step 2.1 tends to zero in $L^2$ and hence in $L^1$ by [F5]. The elementary bound $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the derivative of $e^{iu}$ along the real interval, makes its effect on each characteristic function tend to zero. Combine steps 2.2 and 3.2: $\mathbb Ee^{itT_n/\sqrt n}\to e^{-t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}$ for every real $t$. Under [A1], [F7] identifies this with the characteristic function of $N(0,\sigma_Z^2)$, and [F8] gives the asserted weak convergence. This remains valid for $\sigma_Z^2=0$; all finite-moment and discarded-set assertions were already proved in step 1.1.

The invertible left shift $T(x)_i=x_{i+1}$ preserves $Q$. Put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$ and $\mathcal G_k=\sigma(X_i:i\ge k)$. For every integer $k$, every $n\ge1$, and real square-integrable $U$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $V$ measurable in $\mathcal G_{k+n}$,
$$|\operatorname{Cov}_Q(U,V)|\le\rho_Y(n)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(U)\operatorname{Var}_Q(V)}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence, with $|Z_0|\le B$ almost surely for a finite $B$, and suppose
$$\sum_{r=1}^\infty\alpha_Z(r)<\infty.$$
Put $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$. Then its covariance series converges absolutely and
$$\sigma_Z^2=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r=1}^\infty\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(T_n)}n\ge0.$$
Moreover
$$T_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Z^2),$$
including $\sigma_Z^2=0$. Writing $D_Z=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)|$, every finite subset $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right)^2\le D_Z|I|.$$
The strong-mixing coefficient is that of [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, square-integrable real process ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and put $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$. If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$ and
$$\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k=0,$$
then $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nY_k\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in distribution to $N(0,0)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $Q=Q_{Y_0}$ for the absolute tail quantile in [F2], and put $w(u)=1+\sum_{r\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{u<\alpha_Y(r)\}}$ and $J=\int_0^1w(u)Q(u)^2\,du$. We first show in every stated regime that $J<\infty$ and $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. In regime 1, $Q\le B$ and [F5] give $J\le B^2(1+\sum_r\alpha_Y(r))<\infty$. This regime also already follows directly from [F1].

In regime 2 put $p=2+\delta$ and $\theta=1-2/p=\delta/(2+\delta)\in(0,1)$. Holder's inequality [F6] with exponents $p/2$ and $p/(p-2)$, followed by the quantile identity [F2], gives
$$\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta\left(\int_0^1Q(u)^p\,du\right)^{2/p}=\alpha_Y(r)^\theta(\mathbb E|Y_0|^p)^{2/p}.$$
Tonelli [F5] and the assumed summability yield $J<\infty$. Also $0\le\alpha_Y(r)\le1$ by its event definition, so $\alpha_Y(r)\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta$, proving unweighted summability.

In regime 3, choose constants $C<\infty$ and $a\in(0,1)$ so $\alpha_Y(r)\le Ca^r$ outside a finite set of lags. Counting the positive integers satisfying $u<Ca^r$ shows $w(u)\le C_1+C_2\log(1/u)$ for $0<u<1$, with finite nonnegative constants $C_1,C_2$; also $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. Set $x=Q(u)^2$ and $v=\tfrac12\log(1/u)$, then integrate and use [F2]:
$$\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log(1/u)\,du\le2\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log^+(Q(u)^2)\,du+2\int_0^1u^{-1/2}\,du=4\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]+4<\infty.$$
Together with the assumed second moment this proves $J<\infty$. Thus the two properties announced in step 1.1 hold in all three regimes, without imposing a power moment in regime 3.

Let $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_r)$. By [F2], [F12] and [F5],
$$\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|\le4\sum_{r\ge1}\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du=4\int_0^1(w(u)-1)Q(u)^2\,du<\infty.$$
Set $D_Y=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|$. Expanding a finite centered sum over $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ and counting at most $|I|$ pairs at each positive lag gives $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Y_i)^2\le D_Y|I|$. For consecutive sums the exact expression is $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant and [F4] prove convergence to the stated $\sigma_Y^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of nonnegative variances.

For an integer $M\ge1$ put $c_M(y)=\max(-M,\min(y,M))$, $Z_k^{(M)}=c_M(Y_k)-\mathbb Ec_M(Y_0)$, and $H_M(y)=y-c_M(y)$. Then $R_k^{(M)}=Y_k-Z_k^{(M)}=H_M(Y_k)-\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)$. Both processes are strictly stationary by [F3], and $Z^{(M)}$ is centered and bounded by $2M$. Its coefficients are bounded by $\alpha_Y$, whose sum is finite by steps 1.1–1.3. Thus [F1] gives an absolutely convergent covariance series with nonnegative sum $\sigma_M^2$, normalized variance convergence to $\sigma_M^2$, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_M^2)$.

Put $t_M=\mathbb P(|Y_0|>M)$ and let $Q_{H_M}$ be the absolute quantile of $H_M(Y_0)$. Since $|H_M(Y_0)|=(|Y_0|-M)_+\le|Y_0|$, monotonicity of tail probabilities gives $Q_{H_M}(u)\le Q(u)$, while $Q_{H_M}(u)=0$ for $u\ge t_M$ by its defining infimum. $$D_{R^{(M)}}:=\mathbb E(R_0^{(M)})^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(R_0^{(M)},R_r^{(M)})|\le8\int_0^{t_M}w(u)Q(u)^2\,du=:e_M^2.$$
Here the integrand is integrable by steps 1.1–1.3, and $t_M\to0$ because $Y_0$ is finite almost surely; hence [F4] makes $e_M\to0$. Using the variance limits in steps 2.1 and 2.2 yields $|\sigma_Y-\sigma_M|\le e_M$, where the square roots are nonnegative. Therefore $\sigma_M\to\sigma_Y$.

For fixed real $t$, $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the unit-modulus derivative along the real interval, and [F7] give $|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-\mathbb Ee^{it\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}/\sqrt n}|\le |t|e_M$. By the CLT in step 2.2 and [F9], the second characteristic function tends to $e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}$, identified by [F8]. Consequently
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|\le |t|e_M+|e^{-t^2\sigma_M^2/2}-e^{-t^2\sigma_Y^2/2}|.$$
Let $M\to\infty$ and apply step 3.1. Under [A1], [F8]–[F9] prove $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$. The case $\sigma_Y^2=0$ is also independently supplied by [F10] using absolute covariance summability from step 2.1. All three regimes and the degenerate case follow.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$
